Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 39, to amend the Act to authorize rearrangements and transfers of duties in the public service.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to add a section to the statute passed in 1918, an act to authorize rearrangements and transfers of duties in the public service. The section provides that the powers, duties and functions assigned to the minister and officers of the branch from which the transfer is made shall automatically be vested in the minister and the officers of the department to which the transfer is made. A similar provision exists in statutes with respect to particular departments, and it is the suggestion of the commissioners having to do with the revision of the statutes that this section should be made general to secure clearness and uniformity.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES

speechtext: Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from the end of steel at Mile 24 on the Melfort Northeasterly line of the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Railway to Mile 41 near Nip-awin, in the province of Saskatchewan; mileage already graded, 6 miles; estimated mileage including existing grading, 17 miles; estimated cost, $360,000.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

I suppose the
'Minister of Railways proposes to take advantage of this opportunity to read the necessary parts from a letter of the president of the National Railway System.

I would not think that
would be necessary as the construction of this line was supported by my hon. friend. We are just adding a little to it. My hon. friend must have had all of that information last year.

I should think
my hon .friend would like to have a proper record.

I should be delighted to
give the information but it will not be from a letter of the president. The information I have on the subject is as follows:
Melfort N.E., Mile 24-41	Cost
Grade now ahead of track, 6 miles Proposed in 1924, 11 miles grade;
17 miles track	$360,000
It is proposed in 1924 to add 11 miles of grading to the existing 6 miles ahead of the track and lay the steel on this 17 miles, taking the line to near the town of Nipawin, at an estimated cost of $360,000. When this work is completed, it is proposed to leave the track there for some years.
The first work done on this line in 1919, when the grading was started, 30 miles of which was completed by' the end of the season 1920, the track being laid on 23.7 miles in 1921, and 1922 the ballasting, etc., being finished that far.
The line runs through a particularly good agricultural area, admirably suited for grain growing and the proposed extension would take the branch into the heart of a large settlement very well developed. The grain off this line is its justification, it being figured that 612,000 bushels annually might be expected, besides which 140 cars of freight inbound and outbond, consisting of live stock, coal lumber, merchandise and wood, would be furnished the line. Practically all of these commodities, and particularly the grain and live stock, give a long haul to the

railway, thus supplying other lines of the system with considerable business.
It is estimated that the average saving in distance for road haul to the farmers for their grain would be 12 miles, and if this is taken to be worth | cents per bushel per mile hauled, on the estimated quantity of 612,000 bushels this would make a saving annually to the farmers of $55,080 on the grain alone.
This is one of the lines in which the grading was done on the branch line arrangement, I think, of 1919.

I take it this
year's programme will complete the railway to Nipawin.
That is about it-near the town of Nipawin.

In this particular case I think a large amount of money has already been spent on the line. This line if built, when built, will be a very great advantage to a very good agricultural part of the country, and it seems to me the system is absolutely committed to its construction. Further than that I believe the construction is a good one. It is one which of itself ought to go on.	'

I would like to refer in a general way to the question of these Canadian National branch lines, and, to bring the matter within the purview of the House, and in order to let the House know where I stand in this matter, I propose to read from the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway for 1923, presented to the shareholders in March last in the city of Montreal. This report is signed by the president of the Company, E. W. Beatty, and the president takes his stand in regard to railway expansion for his system. I am in favour of the National railway being also given every fair facility to expand where the requirements of the country call for it, and I intend to keep to a like position for the expansion of the Canadian National. I was one of those who favoured the acquirement of the Canadian National Railways and I advocated it in days gone by. Now that we have the Canadian National railways, this House is bound, in every fair way, if the proper extension is a proper one, to vote the money for it, and I think if the extensions are reasonable they should be made. In order to show the position of the Canadian Pacific Railway on this question, I will read from the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway for the fiscal year ending 31st December, 1923, dated Montreal, March, 1924. Section 5 reads:

C.N.R.-Branch Lilies
Owing to the magnitude of your system, continuous expenditures on capital account will always be necessary, if it is to keep pace with the growing transportation requirements of the country but your directors have adhered to the policy of restricting the issuance of securities to the lowest amount, consistent with the maintenance of the property. During the year under review the fixed charges were increased only by the modest sum of $121,747, and dividends payable on preference stock by the sum of $447,732.
Then he goes on to name the roads which he is in favour of, and he names those which are practical for immediate construction, or construction as soon as possible. He mentions the following:
Leader southerly branch, mileage 50 to 75.
Lomond northwesterly extension of the Suffield southwesterly branch, mileage 30 to 40.
An extension of the Archive-Wymark branch to Coderre, 12 miles.
An extension of the Moose Jaw southwesterly branch from Consul easterly, mileage 60 to mileage 97. Amulet-Dunkirk branch 25 miles.
The requisite applications to parliament are being made for the necessary statutory authority to construct such of the above lines, the charter authorities for which have expired or are expiring.
Arrangements have been made for the construction of an extension of the Tuffnell-Prince Albert branch of the Manitoba and North Western Railway from mileage 50 to mileage 129. The Manitoba and North Western Railway Company has statutory authority to issue bonds not exceeding $40,000 per mile in respect of this branch, which bonds will in the usual course be acquired by this company with the proceeds of the sale of consolidated debenture stock to be issued for the purpose.
That means that the Canadian Pacific Railway at its directors' meeting announced that they intended to continue their policy of extension of their lines, and the great magnitude of the system was their justification. Does that argument not also apply to the Canadian National Railways? I say that when the Canadian Pacific Railway is embarking on these various propositions the Canadian National Railways should not be held back. Here we have the Canadian Pacific Railway proposing this policy of extension; the announcement is made at the annual meeting of the directors, and the shareholders approved of it. This same argument applies still more to the Canadian National system, which is a larger road, a consolidation of a great many other roads, and is now coming to be the great National Railway of Canada.
Since this discussion opened we have heard rather queer things in connection with the Canadian National Railways. I am going to refer to the speech made in this House by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). Less than twelve days ago he made a speech in which he dealt
with this question of the extension of the Canadian National, and he told us a rather doleful tale. First of all, he made a calculation, and placed it before the House, as to what the commitments of Canada in connection with all our National Railways were, and at page 896 of Hansard hon. members will find a summary of those commitments as he gives them, amounting to two billion dollars. He said they would be even more than that. Now if the amount of the commitments of Canada on account of the Canadian Nationals is to be quoted in this House, it is high time this House settled in some way what the commitments are and what would be a fair interest on them. So,
I am going to make a suggestion. The prime minister of England made a suggestion of this kind not so long ago which was accepted. Let us admit that the statement of the hon. member is correct, and that we have this debt of two billion dollars on account of the National Railways; let us fix the amount of interest, and then we will know what the annual charge is to be. It would not be a bad calculation for us to call it a billion and a half for these commitments, and allow three per cent on that. That means that the Canadian National will have to make sixty million dollars a year above its working expenses in order to pay its way. Let us put the amount at a million dollars a week. Let us therefore take this amount for a starting point in this House and the country-that we are committed to at least a million dollars a week out of the earnings of the National Railway to pay the commitments after the overhead has been paid. I think this would be a very fair proposal, because all that money did not actually go into the building on the various roads-the old Intercolonial, the old Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and a dozen other roads that have disappeared into the consolidation. These roads are all in this consolidation and all are in this estimate of the member for St. Lawrence-St. George. It is an absurd estimate to place the figure at two billion dollars, though the hon. member said it was more than that. Let us put it at a billion and a half, and count that practically a million dollars a week should be set aside out of the earning expenses to pay the interest on this investment. When we have that, we have something to go on, and I challenge the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the Minister of Railways, to
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

come to an understanding in this House, in order to settle once and for all the amount to be recognized as the interest charges of the National Railways, as against its earnings, after the cost of running the road has been paid.
The hon. member (Mr. Marler) at page 898 of Hansard, madte this remarkable statement :
In conclusion as regards the remarks which I have been making I want to say this-and it has reference to a fact which, I think, is not fully understood or fully grasped-we have in this country at present two great railway systems, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific.
I grant that.
I think every member in this House, I think everybody in this country, should wish well for both these lines, they are both great national undertakings.
I dispute that. The Canadian National Railway system is the only national undertaking in this country. It is owned by the Canadian people, the Canadian Pacific is owned by a private company under a charter granted by parliament a good many years ago, it is capitalized at over a billion dollars, and has a great earning capacity. Nobody knows who may be the next owners of the Canadian Pacific. I have some reasons for suspecting that certain American railways have tried to acquire the Canadian Pacific-perhaps they could acquire it to-morrow. Either the Pennsylvania Railway or the New York Central Railway might acquire the Canadian Pacific to-morrow, and the ownership would pass out of the hands of-I was going to say Canadians, but there are other stockholders in Europe. On the other hand, the Canadian people own the Canadian National Railways and intend to keep them forever. Therefore, I dispute the hon. member's statement that the Canadian Pacific is a national railway on a parity with the Canadian National. It is not. The only hold that we have to-day on the Canadian Pacific is through a most peculiar clause in the charter creating the Company, a clause which I do not think was ever incorporated in any other railway legislation. This clause is to the effect that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is to maintain the railway in the interests of the people of Canada for ever. That is why the American roads to-day have not secured the Canadian Pacific railway. They do not like to undertake the responsibility of maintaining the road in the interests of the Canadian people for ever.
The hon. member also made this surprising statement:
Now to have competition between these two lines is senseless in the extreme. If traffic arrangements can be made with one line to help out another line, I 
think those arrangements should be made. To build lines unnecessarily when there is not enough traffic to satisfy both these systems is not putting this House, is not putting this country, in a position to get lower freight rates in the very slightest degree.
The hon. member proposes co-operation between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National with respect to branch lines. Does it not follow that some day the two systems will be consolidated? I know many people in the W est say it is a good thing for the country that we have railway competition. Perhaps it is, but it may entail very heavy and needless expense. Therefore, I believe that when the people realize what their commitments are for these two great systems, they will come to see that there is something in the argument advanced by the hon. member and that through the elimination of competition great economies may be effected. I think this is the first time that anyone has heard-shall I say?-a "cry from Macedonia," -a suggestion from Montreal, in favour of co-operation between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. Perhaps somebody is getting frightened about the future. Undoubtedly, the progress of the Canadian National is the surprise of the world to-day, and its position is a credit to the Conservative party that consolidated its component roads into one great system.
As one who has done something in that direction, I am going to support any reasonable proposal for branch line development of the Canadian National Railways after this declaration by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. Beatty, endorsed by his shareholders, in favour of a similar development of their system to look after the transportation needs of the Dominion. I agree with the leader of the opposition that there should be a careful scrutiny of the proposals that come before this House for building branch lines as feeders for our great national railway system, but I would sooner retire from this House than acquiesce in the proposal that the Canadian Pacific shall be allowed to expand but that the Canadian National must expand no further. We have a right to proceed with a programme of expansion, even if we have to go in debt to finance it, for there is no doubt that the position of the road is absolutely sound.
I have always had complete confidence in Sir Henry Thornton. That confidence does not extend to his co-directors,-but he did not appoint them. I am still a believer in the management of our National system by a board of directors such as was authorized and established by the Conservative party.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
This House has always maintained control of the National system in its review of any proposals which may come from the management. Therefore, until I hear some real objection to these branch lines I am going to give reasonable support to the proposals and that we at least keep faith with our people by extending the system wherever extension may be needed. I would give especial preference to the West in this respect. I think all these branch lines will eventually pay their way.
But here is the great difference between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National system. The Canadian Pacific is a privately owned line, committed to the payment of dividends to its stockholders. I hope that the ambition of the men who administer the Canadian National Railways is to give service at the lowest possible rates irrespective of dividends. That is a rather rabid doctrine, perhaps it may be termed Red or Bolshevik, but it seems to me that the people desire a national system of railways so operated as to render a service at minimum rates instead of piling up big dividends for shareholders. Therefore, I repeat that I disagree with the statement of the hon. member for St. Lawrence St. George that the two roads are of the same "breed of dog." They are absolutely different. One is the people's road;	the other
is owned and controlled outside of Canada-by whom, we do not know. The Canadian Pacific Railway could be acquired in New York or in London to-morrow, and that is a significant fact which the Canadian people have to consider. Therefore, to ask me to refrain from endorsing any reasonable proposal for the expansion of the Canadian National Railways while the Canadian Pacific is allowed to go on is something to which I cannot agree. So I say that if the Canadian Pacific Railway is going ahead we should keep pace mile for mile, if that can be justified, as I hope it will.
There is another public owner of railways in this Dominion and that is my own province of Ontario. That province has built a splendid road in the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, which is opening up new mining country. That road has been paid for, by the people of Ontario, and it is believed pretty generally that the Canadian National Railways to-morrow would take it over, assuming all the liabilities in connection with it and giving all the extensions which the people require in northern Ontario. Doing that, of course, they would also no doubt afford similar extensions in the province of Quebec.
The railways in Canada are operated at present on a most primitive basis; their locomotion depends upon the generation of steam in individual engines. This is not the most satisfactory way of operating railways. So far as I can gather, the best railway experts to-day are to be found in England, and it is their opinion that as the railways in that country cannot be driven by hydro energy, then the electrical power can be generated by great batteries in connection with boilers situated right at the mouth of the coal pit. Electricity generated in that way could drive all the railways in England at a lower cost than they can be operated to-day; and I have no doubt that this is what will be done with the five systems of railways in England. In England the best engineers are working out the problem of the electrification of the railways upon the bases of high tension and long distance transmission. Electrical energy can be transmitted almost a thousand miles now without any great waste. In this country we could electrify our railways and provide energy for all our industries, and I think that steps ought to be taken to bring this about. We have in Canada, from British Columbia, right through the western provinces, through Ontario and Quebec, a number of rivers which could provide electrical energy to drive every mile of railway in the Dominion, and drive it at a much lower cost than the railways are being driven at the present time. Already, I believe, the two great systems in Canada have given some consideration to this question; but no private concern could undertake a work of this character in the way that a nation could. In any event, it would be well if the two railways could get together and co-operate in this direction; and for the first time we have heard some suggestion from Montreal which would seem to indicate that the Canadian Pacific Railway is not averse to action of this kind. This of course is only what some people might call a "gesture"; but at any rate it seems to me to convey some significance. At least I should like to see some co-operation between the province of Ontario and the Canadian National Railways, because there is no reason why the construction of rival lines should continue. In my opinion there ought to be some consolidation of railway service in the mining districts in Quebec and Ontario. The Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway and the Canadian National Railways, from North Bay, through Sudbury and in that direction, might with advantage be consolidated. If the Canadian Pacific Railway were willing to co-operate, so much the better; but at any rate it would be well, I think, to have such a consolidation of the roads in the prov-

ince of Ontario as I have indicated. There is a great demand for economy to-day, and I am glad to have heard from my hon. friend (Mr. Marler) that he is prepared to support a policy of co-operation.
As to the future of the Canadian National Railways, let me say that the principle of public ownership has been adopted in this country as a permanent institution. The people of Canada own the National Railways now and are determined to make them a success. To do this they are going to patronize the national roads before any other railway. In Ontario, apart from the public ownership of railways, we have a publicly owned hydro electric system which has been exceedingly successful. It has paid all its commitments and is meeting its interest charges in the way of amortization and so forth. Some years ago, I might remark here, a company was organized to build a- railway and power service in Brazil. Millions of dollars were put into that concern and stock was sold in Canada, although there was never any very great return from it. Three gentlemen in Ontario have now undertaken the revival of this Brazilian road and the first step they have taken in the matter, is, to me, the greatest compliment, on the part of a private concern, to public ownership. Mr. Couzens, who was formerly general manager of the Toronto Transportation Company, a publicly-owned street railway, and who was also general manager of the HydroElectric System of Ontario, was offered and accepted a position with these parties who are now developing the Brazilian road. Mr. Couzens was bred to public ownership in England, and in this country he was a strong advocate of the principle. He is the ablest technical man in railways in America to-day, and these people offered him a considerable inducement in the way of salary to join them. I do not blame him for going; he is a man who is getting up in years and pro-
4 p.m. bably in five years' time he will be in easy circumstances. I do not know whether the city of Toronto had the opportunity of retaining Mr. Couzens, but I believe that they would give three times what they are now paying out to have kept him. It was rather significant that so soon as he went out of office-and no one knew that he was going until his resignation was submitted-the city of Toronto secured two young men, trained in the University of Toronto, our own boys, to take charge of the public transportation system and of the power distribution system as well. We are bringing up these men by the score in our universities and they are all ardent advocates of public ownership. They would rather see the public

utilities improved than that these things should be operated for the purpose of creating earnings for shareholders of over-capitalized corporations. We have a good start in public ownership in Ontario and are making considerable headway with the Toronto transportation system. Hon. gentlemen have only to consider the success that has attended the Hydro system, and to look at the success which the Canadian National Railways are meeting, to be convinced of the benefits of public ownership. The success of the Canadian National Railways is a surprise to the world. Is it not reasonable, then, to suppose that the United States, in view of this fact, and seeing what a revolution has swept over not only this country but England and other places as well, will follow suit? Let us hold w'hat we have, I say, and keep pace with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
My hon. friend (Mr. Marler) made a doleful but very able speech; I read it in a sick bed some days ago, and I was pleased to read it. I give my hon. friend credit for it, but it was a brief for the Canadian Pacific Railway. Apparently the brief was cut in two, because the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) afterwards got up and endorsed every word that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said. Then he went on. Anyway, who is Esau? Ask the member for St. Lawrence-St. George. Or ask the member for Joliette; perhaps he knows. So, that after all the struggles of the past, after all the stones that have been thrown at the government for consolidating these roads, we have them now and we are at least going to keep step with the Canadian Pacific. I do not know whether the minister has had an opportunity of reading the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but there is his justification.
I have a copy of it.

I suggest that
hon. members get their copy of this annual report and read it. It may be said that we have not the money to do these things, but if the Canadian Pacific can afford it the people of Canada can afford it; that is my answer to that argument. The Canadian Pacific is a great railway. It has enormous resources, it has good management and a splendid board of directors. But the Canadian National as it is to-day has seventy per cent of the strategical advantage of the transcontinental railways of this country.

They have it at Montreal, acquired by the Grand Trunk, sixty or seventy years ago. They have it in the St. Lawrence district, at Toronto, in the Niagara river district. Their advantage in those sections is so great that the New York Central had to duplicate their lines right through. The Grand Trunk crossed the Detroit river and carried that strategical advantage right to Chicago, and the greatest earning railway in Canada to-day is the old Grand Trunk between Chicago and the St. Lawrence and New England ports. We also have a lot of the strategical advantage of the West. We have it in the mining country of northern Ontario, in the ownership of either the Dominion or the province. We have the advantage also in the Rocky mountains. Our pass is the best pass through the Rockies, and we would share it on terms with the Canadian Pacific if they should feel like approaching us. We hear a lot of talk about the harbour of Vancouver, but there is another harbour called Prince Rupert, and it is going to be one of the great ports of the Pacific, so we have the strategical advantage there too. It is true we have to cross the Canadian Pacific tracks to get to Vancouver, but some day that may be adjusted. The National Railways are surprising the world to-day by their success and by the excellence of their administration. I would like to point out also that it might be conceived that if the Canadian Pacific Board became dissatisfied with this country they might undertake to sell their road on the New York or London market. Of course they say it is the last thing they would do, that they are actuated by national reasons in maintaining the line as it is. But the temptation is always there to take the money for it, to cash in and distribute the proceeds among the shareholders. They would make that distribution to-morrow but for the wise provision made by Sir John A. Macdonald. Nobody knows why he did it, but for all time the condition is imposed on the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to maintain that road for the service of the people of Canada. Whether or not in a court of law they could be made to deliver the goods I do not know, but it certainly is the one thing that keeps the Americans from buying out the Canadian Pacific.	.
I say to the Minister of Railways, go on with your extensions wherever they can be justified, wherever the president can give a substantial reason for the expansion of the system. I believe that the Canadian people, including a great many Conservatives, will support him in a policy of that kind.

I want to compliment the
hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) upon the manner in which he has faithfully and, if I may say so, tenaciously, stuck to his belief in public ownership. If any man in this House deserves the title of father of public ownership of railways, I think it is the hon. member for South York.
The district through which this branch line goes, forms part of the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and cannot I feel sure, be surpassed in productiveness in any part of the West. The people went in there some fifteen or twenty years ago and settled forty-five miles, or even further than that, from the nearest railway. They did so, of course, in the belief that the railway would ultimately go through, but during all these years they have been hauling their grain long distances. In 1921 this twenty-four miles of line was built from Melfort to Ridgedale. Even before the steel was laid, elevators were going up, but no sooner did the steel get through than elevators sprang up at the three stations on that piece of line, almost over night-sprang up like mushrooms. I am sure that they have been a paying proposition ever since. It is now intended to extend this line out to Nipawin, a distance of another seventeen miles, six of which are already graded. I know the district very well, and have no hesitation in saying that this extension will be a paying proposition. There is just one thing that occurs to me: There is a district out further east which is likely to be left without transportation service. A delegation came down here last year to make representations in the matter and I had hopes that some provision would be made for service there. This line going up to Nipawin will still be a considerable distance from the district further east to which I refer. We do not want our railway lines to parallel each other. The Canadian Pacific has a charter through this country and I think we should keep in mind that the lines should be as far apart as possible so that some one of them will give a service to the people to the east. That country to the east is very thickly settled and very productive, but a great many of the people still have to haul their grain a considerable distance. I shall not speak at any further length except to say that there can be no doubt whatever as to the advisability of getting a line through this district.

There is something like 40,000 acres of grain which will be marketed in Neidpath providing the elevator can be built so as to store the grain until it can be got out. I would like the minister to give me that assurance so that the farmers can go ahead with the arrangements for building the elevator with the certainty of being able to take out the grain this fall.
Mr. Reid: In speaking to Mr. Hanna about the matter he mentioned that they would lay this ten miles this year for the reason that an elevator would
CN.R.-Branch Lines

be built, and it was for that purpose the rails would be laid. I am quite satisfied that it is the intention of the Canadian National Railway management to lay the ten miles in question and I feel satisfied from the way Mr. Hanna mentioned it to me that there is no doubt it will be done. Unless something unforeseen should happen it is the intention anyway to lay the rails before that time. The 50,000 tons of new rails which were purchased are now being rolled and sent on to the main line. The rails thus released will go on to the branch lines and the branch in question is one of those that will be taken up first.
So hon. members will see that the people had been promised this line for several years. Now there is a prospect of its being completed. When introducing this resolution the Minister of Railways stated that this line would be completed this year, but that the branch line programme is to extend over three years. I would ask him, does this preclude the possibility of any further extension of the line for the next three years?

Of course, every session
parliament can do as it pleases. It depends on the programme approved by parliament and on the recommendation made by the Canadian National Railway Board as to the necessity of the line.

That, of course, is the crux of the whole question. The minister spoke of the psychological effect that a three year programme would have upon people in the vicinity of the projected line when they became aware that railway construction would proceed for the next three years. I wonder what the psychological effect will be when the people find that the line may not be completed during the next three years. I would urge upon the minister the necessity of proceeding with the construction as rapidly as possible. I shall submit various reasons in support of my request, and I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) will back me up.
In the first place, if to-day the people affected wish to bring in coal or fruit from the West they must haul it 265 miles. That is to say, it must be hauled from Swift Current to Moose Jaw, then round by Gravelbourg and up to Neidpath, a distance of 265 miles; whereas if this gap were constructed, the haul would be only twenty-four miles. This is not good business, and undoubtedly great economy would be effected if the gap were spanned. It is very difficult for us to get fruit on the prairies. On the Gravelbourg extension line we have a tri-weekly service, and by the time perishable goods have been hauled the 265 miles they are in such bad condition that the people are discouraged and do not attempt to ship in fruit which they require. I honestly believe that if this 
line were completed it would pay for itself in one year lay reason of the increased freight business that would necessarily follow. At the present time we are advocating the shipment of grain via Vancouver. The country tributary to this line grows, as the hon. minister has already stated, 480,000 bushels of wheat every year. Under present conditions if we wish to send our grain to Vancouver we would have to pay freight rate on an extra 265 miles. I believe the time is coming when the people in the district will send their grain westward to Vancouver, and there is no reason why they should not have the opportunity of doing so by the spanning of this gap. Furthermore, this territory is naturally tributary to Swift Current. Swift Current is the logical distributing centre, but owing to the noncompletion of this branch line the farmers in the neighbourhood have to rely on Moose Jaw, which means a longer haul of 265 miles. I might cite many other reasons in support of my request, but I do not wish to weary the committee. I think the minister knows that the gap should be bridged at as early a date as possible, and I hope that in the very near future he will see to it that the necessary construction is proceeded with. I hope also that the Minister of Agriculture, who knows the district well and has often had delegations wait upon him about the completion of this line, will also back me up in this request.

Mr. Chairman, the recital by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) of the necessity for the completion of this branch line is, I think, substantially correct. It was a bitter disappointment a year ago to the people along the prospective route to find that, notwithstanding that a construction crew with full equipment and material was already on the ground, the whole thing had to be called off. The result was that the people had to wait a year longer, and I am sure that it is generally hoped that there will not be a recurrence of what one might regard as almost a catastrophe to people who have been waiting so many years for a much needed railway service. As regards the suggested extension to Swift Current, that gap of course should be bridged as soon as possible. But as the board could not exceed the mileage of last year the question with them, as I presume it must be with all of us, was, how best to expend the money, primarily to the advantage of the farmers themselves. I do not like to make any comparisons as between the various interests of the farmers and the cities, but I

CJV.R.-Branch Lines
think hon. gentlemen will agree that the primary object in the building of many of the branch lines was to place the farmers sufficiently near their markets to make it possible for them to grow grain at a profit and without spending all their earnings in wagon and sleigh haulage. I am afraid, notwithstanding the claims made in regard to this extension, that there are some . outstanding rural districts that have even stronger claims.
I may refer to one or two in Saskatchewan west of Shell Brook. The hon. member for Prince Albert is not in his seat, but some other hon. gentlemen who are present know what a vast extent of territory lies west of Shell Brook, into the Mistawasis district, past Shell river and into Norquay, a distance of some 50 miles. The whole of this district has been settled and there is not a railway within 40 or 50 miles of these people. There is another line west of Turtleford that requires to be extended; there should be an extension through the Paradise Hill country in the province of Alberta, and something should be done in that case at an early date. The question is, which of these various claims is the most urgent? It is important, I think, that the gap between Neid-path and the city of Swift Current should be bridged, because it would save a tremendous haul for grain, coal and lumber coming from the West; and the people of Swift Current would themselves appreciate the speedy building of this road, for it would mean a very great deal to them. As' to what next year will bring forth, that of course is something that must depend upon the results of this year's work and the speed with which the present programme is carried out.

The attitude
we take towards this line is precisely the attitude we took in connection with some of the other branch lines:	it is one that should
have been built last year, and could have been built if the government had taken the matter up as a question of business. The delay is to be attributed in part to the Minister >
of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) as a member of the cabinet, and all the pretence and sham about the three-j'ear period is extremely obvious in this case. We have no objection to this proposal.

This line does not
run through my constituency but I am familiar with the territory which it is intended to serve. I understand that the line was projected originally to extend as far west as Swift Current. The line has been completed with the exception of a gap of
24 miles, and, as has been explained by the hon. member for Swift Current, this gap necessitates a tremendous haul, of from 200 to 250 miles, of coal and lumber coming from British Columbia. My impression is that until the gap is bridged the line of railway as it stands at present will not pay. Has th'e board made any recommendation that the line not so far built be completed at an early date?

All recommendations
made will be found in the branch lines programme.

The justification for building this line is that about $110,000 has already been invested in the grading now done, which is earning no money, and it is estimated that 396,000 bushels of grain per year will be hauled off the line when completed. Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from Hanna to Warden in the province of Alberta; estimated mileage including existing grading, 57 miles; estimated cost, $1,445,000.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

The following is the statement with respect to this branch line:
In 1924 it is proposed to grade 57 miles of this at a cost of $504,500, and in 1925 to lay track on this 57 miles of grade, and ballast 30 miles at a cost of $792,000. In 1926 it is proposed to ballast 27 miles at a cost of $148,500 thus completing the branch.
Construction of this line will serve a double purpose, as it will open up the agricultural district through which it will run and will also make a shorter route for railway and other coal to Hanna and points east, as well as shortening the route from points on the Goose Lake line to points northwest.
The country through which this line runs is a good agricultural area, principally grain raising, and there is considerable settlement and development throughout.	.	,
The justification for the construction of this line is that about $42,000 per year will be saved in routing coal, and that there will be 1,710,000 bushels of grain marketed on this line, besides 370 cars of in and out bound freight consisting of live stock, coal, lumber and merchandise. It is figured that on the average, 12 miles of road haul will be saved to the farmers, and this applied to the 1,710,000 bushels of grain and taken as being worth l cents per bushel per mile hauled, will mean an annual saving to the farmers of $153,900 in road haul on grain alone. The class of freight produced from this line, being all of a long haul character, will contribute business to other lines of the system.

I am not rising to
oppose this line, part of it lying through the country I happen to represent, but I do wish to present one or two facts in connection with it to the committee, and for the consideration of the minister.
As far as cheapening of operating costs in transporting coal is concerned, I am not competent to discuss it from that point of view.
I know, however, that the saving will be considerable. A large part of the coal loaded at the Brazeau collieries will be routed that way, I think. When you consider that about 16,000 cars were loaded at Brazeau in 1923

CJVJf.-Branch Lines
you can see the possibilities in that direction. The comments which I wish to make, however, are in regard to the location of the line as it affects the farming territory to be served, and while I am not in any way attempting to set my opinion against the opinion of the engineers who laid out this line I would suggest from my knowledge of the country there that they take into consideration these facts.
The line proposed runs from Hanna to Warden. If the line proposed ran from Hanna to Big Valley, about 16 miles south of Warden, and be taken in connection with the proposed line in the next resolution, from Loverna westward, which will ultimately connect up with the Hanna-Warden or Hanna-Big Valley branch, the distance would be shortened and I believe the country served would be a more fertile country and would produce a larger amount of freight. In connection with that may I make one suggestion? I have, of course, as have all other hon. members, received a great many requests for branch lines, and I have always asked the farmers when they made such a request that they accompany it with a map showing all the farms located within a ten-mile radius on either side of the line, together with the amount of produce of various kinds available for shipment that they have produced in the last two or three years.

The hon. member speaks
of combining this line with the other line. Would it take the same distance, 107 miles, if they were combined, or would it shorten the distance?

As far as the distance
is concerned, if the two lines were combined, the distance would be shorter in every case if the terminus of the present branch were at Big Valley instead of Warden.

And serve as good a
country?

And serve a more
fertile and a more thickly settled country, as the part of the country chosen for the proposed route is more or less of a lake country, and is partly used for cattle grazing. I am speaking now of the point with which I am acquainted, that is the farming country to be served and the farm produce to be expected as freight. I am not referring to the shorter routing of coal, which, of course, is an argument on the other side, and if there is a distinct advantage to be derived by the railways in that respect and from other sources it would, of course, overweigh the service rendered to the farmer. But I am
speaking from the point of view of the farmers to be served, in order that these facts may be given consideration in arriving at a conclusion. I am not prepared at the moment, the map being a very extensive one, to give definite data of the amount of produce to be expected. The data is not complete, and I have not a full map showing that. I am merely throwing out as a suggestion that this procedure might well be adopted when any lines are projected, that a township map be prepared showing the farmers resident on each quarter section within that ten-mile radius, and the amount of produce raised and shipped over the railway in the past two or three years. It would involve very little expense to the railway company or to the government. I have found in my own experience that farmers in the vicinity are only too willing to co-operate and give this information at their own expense if necessary.
It would help the committee to form an intelligent conclusion as to the class of territory to be served and the amount of traffic which the road might expect to receive.
There is another point that I think is well worthy of consideration. I am not aware as to how far this projected development will alter the present terminal point. I do not know whether that point will come into consideration at all, but if it does I would like to point out this fact: Big Valley is at present the terminal point; it was constructed as the terminal point. The National Railways have there about a $300,000 development in terminal equipment. The town itself being built largely to house Canadian National Railway employees has provided facilities, educational and otherwise, for those employees. The employees themselves have property which they have purchased, their own homes, amounting to pretty close to $200,000. All of these things I think must be taken into consideration if it is proposed by this short routing to eliminate the divisional point. I have no objection to make if it is in the best interests of the railway that the terminal point should be moved, because I am not here to speak for the interests of one town as opposed to the interests of the system. But again I say, if it is proposed to move the terminal point, to abandon the one already in , existence in favour of another, these facts must be taken into consideration-the amount of loss involved in salvaging the existing equipment, and the amount of compensation which must rightly be paid to the employees if they are removed from their present situation. I think all of these things should be taken cognizance of by the minister, and I hope to have his assurance that these points
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

have been well considered. If they have been well considered, and if it is found that it is more profitable for the railway, because of the shorter routing, to build the line as now projected, I for one have no objections to make. Warden is in my own constituency, just as is Big Valley, so it is nothing to me personally which point is chosen, but I do wish to see the greatest amount of service rendered to the country through which this line will run, and the greatest amount of benefit derived by the line running through that territory.
May I be permitted, in conclusion, to say that there are three things that must be taken into consideration in' building branch lines. The first one, in which we will all agree, is that through bettering, cheapening, shortening existing routes for freight a saving would be made which will pay the interest and sinking fund upon the amount invested by that shortening, cheapening and bettering of existing routes. Second, is the immediate increase of tonnage to be expected from new construction? We are all agreed on that, of course. Then there is the possible increase in tonnage in the future, and when I speak of increased tonnage I do not mean only as applied to branch lines. I have heard many men speak of branch lines as though they should be self-supporting, as though a branch line should be able to show a profit throughout its short length; but to my mind that is not the important point at all. We have to consider every additional ton which can come over a short line and be transferred to the trunk line. We have to consider what that will mean not to the short line, but in its contribution to the trunk lines east and west. To my mind that is a very important point, and a point which some members and some people in the country overlook when they suggest that branch lines should be able to show a profit on their own operation.
Does not most of the traffic get on to the main line anyway?

I have already stated that the justification would be the immediate increase of tonnage, or the increase of tonnage in the future by the development of .the country. I am speaking of increase of tonnage which will find its way to the main line, not to a diversion of tonnage from one branch line to another.
There is another point that must be taken into consideration by this parliament, and that is where this railway differs from the Canadian Pacific or any other privately owned railway. We must take into consideration not only the indirect benefit to be derived by the 
railways but the direct benefit to be derived by the country by the retention of population and an increase in our national prosperity, brought about to some extent at least by more adequate transportation. A privately owned line does not need to take that into consideration, but I believe it is well for us in voting the money of the taxpayers to keep all these points in view. I believe this line will be a profitable line, for I know the country fairly well and the amount of freight that can be expected, but it is for the minister to consider, after taking all these facts into consideration, whether the treminus suggested is the best terminus under all the circumstances.

My hon. friend has
touched on two or three points that are of interest. The people in the vicinity of Big Valley made strong representations along the line that my hon. friend presents. I discussed it at some length with the chairman and with the engineer of construction, Mr. Czowski, and they adhered firmly to this as the best route from the railway standpoint, largely on account of the short hauling of coal. I have no information concerning the suggestion of moving the terminal. That would be a matter for the Canadian National Railway Board, and has not yet been discussed with me. If it has not been repealed, an act was passed by parliament some years ago providing for protection, in a measure, of those railway employees who might be moved from one terminal to another from loss of their property, and so forth. I imagine that law is on the statute book yet, I have had no occasion recently to look it up. Howr-ever, I think the question of terminals was not discussed by the president of the board with me.	,

Has the minister had
the cost of this line confirmed? It seems very low to me.

It is the cost given by
the Canadian National Railway Board, and it is based on the report of their engineers.

Perhaps my hon. friend will give us a rough analysis of this proposition. It is an entirely new proposition. We should know how much is to be spent for right of way, how much for bridges, how much for fills, and how much for rails? If the matter has been at all properly gone into that information has reached the minister's hands.

That detailed information has not been given to me, nor have I

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
attempted to give it to the House in the case of any of these bills. I have never in my life heard it given in detail in relation to any railway construction bill in this House, nor have I ever read of it being given in'any other legislative body.
If such has not been the practice, it is time we started to get down to business.

The memorandum I have here says:
In 1924 it is proposed to grade 57 miles of this at a cost of $504,500 and in 1925 to lay, track on this 57 miles of grade, and ballast 30 miles at a cost of $792,000. In 1926 it is proposed to ballast 27 miles at a cost of $148,500 thus completing the branch.

In reply to the hon.
gentleman (Mr. Marler) as to cost of construction being low, I can give information on that point. I know the territory well and the ground is very level and very solid. Construction can therefore be carried on at a comparatively low cost.

There is this feature of
this line that makes it not quite so imperative as the four lines that have preceded: There is nothing at all done yet, this is an entirely new project. I am convinced from what inquiry I have made-I have not been over the territory, but I have been to within a very few miles of it and learned something about it-that the line should be built, and that it will bring sufficient revenue to justify its construction from the purely railway standpoint. However, I do not think it is as urgent as the four roads covered by the resolutions which have just passed the committee. I have also been urged very strongly with reference to the change in the route from that which I understand was originally contemplated. The reasons have been presented by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), and I do not intend to rehearse them. If, however, there is to be a change involving the transfer of a terminal point or a reduction in the number of divisional points, it is going to be a matter of considerable cost to make good the losses of those who have invested their money in Big Valley, and I see no provision for that in the estimates before the House. It seems to me that it is not something that has to be rushed, and very careful review should be made again as to the wisdom of this change, also on the whole question of the extension. While I am convinced that ordinarily this line should be built and built immediately, these are extraordinary times
and if there is one road in the list that could stand I think this is the one. I urge that consideration upon the minister, but certainly I am convinced the road is a good one and should be built.

The last
speaker, perhaps, is as conversant as we are with the fact that in this district there is a large settlement of returned men. Probably throughout that portion of my constituency there have been more returned men placed on the land than in' any other single block. These men are having a tremendously hard time to make things go.
Where are they located?

East of
Rowley. If they cannot get reasonable railway facilities within the district within a short time it is questionable whether any one of them can stay. I have in my possession at this time answers to a large number of questionnaires and they indicate that one of the most serious causes of the present state of these men is the lack of railway transportation. I join with the last speaker in his very mild criticism of the transfer of the terminal point from Big Valley to Warden. Frankly I would urge that reconsideration be given to that decision. I do not want to place my judgment above that of the engineers in this matter, but I am under the impression that the Canadian National Railway management are guided in this matter by the desire to have a point to which they can have the shortest possible coal haul, leaving aside the possible economies that may be effected by allowing the terminal to remain where it is at Big Valley and where it is giving the best service.
Now, for a moment, allow me to consider the question of the situation of the people of Big Valley themselves. Injustice will unquestionably be done to them by the transference of the terminal point, and therefore the divisional point, from Big Valley to Warden. Last year I asked the minister some questions on this matter but he disclaimed responsibility for it. He pointed out that this was a question of railway policy he did not care to interfere with and he indicated just what the railway company was going to do. I had a discussion subsequently with some of the members of the board of management and they informed me that there was no intention at present to do anything with the divisional point at Big Valley. However, when I got back to Big Valley not much more than a month later, I found the place practically deserted, whilst a feeling of gloom had descended upon everybody there. About 148

Canadian National Railway employees own their homes and lots in the town, and the total assessment on these lands and improvements amounted to $182,100. A number of Canadian National Railway employees who came there in 1922, instead of purchasing lots and building residences lived in box cars, rented rooms, and did other things which were not in the interest of Big Valley on the strength of a rumour that the divisional point was to be removed. So serious a situation arose in consequence, that the town authorities wrote to Mr. A. E. Warren, General Manager, Canadian National Railways, Winnipeg and asked him if this rumour was true. They pointed out that it was essential to meet the liabilities of the school district, which at that time amounted to $31,700, that these men should take up residence in the town and become taxpayers. Mr. Warren replied under date of September 19, 1922, as follows:
Mr. Fred C. Stokes,
Big Valley, Alta.
Dear Sir,
Referring to your letter of August 21, addressed to the Canadian Northern Town Properties Company, Limited, Winnipeg, which was referred to me by* Mr. Field, Land Commissioner, there is no intention of moving the terminal away from Big Valley, so that the rumour referred to cannot be used as a pretext for the employees not buying lots.
As a result of that letter a number of these men then purchased lands and proceeded to erect homes thereon. Not much more than two years later we find they are compelled to abandon their homes and take up jobs somewhere else. That is a serious injustice, and as an hon. gentleman said, no provision has been made to meet that unquestionable liability upon this government. I would ask the minister to take this question into consideration and to see to it that as close a scrutiny be made of this line and its terminal as is possible before the work is proceeded with. I think it is essential in the interests of the country that the work should be proceeded with and the line built. It is needed, but I think the terminal should be Big Valley and not Warden.

I suppose the
minister's idea in regard to coal at this point was the coal from Brazeau. If I am wrong in that I would like to be put right. Surely it cannot be the Drumheller coal. It cannot be anything else but the Brazeau coal. Is that right?
I am taking no exception to the statement.
I am asking as to the coal which is said to be one of the reasons, if not the main reason, for the building of the line. Is it the Brazeau coal?
I think there is no doubt about(it.
What tonnage of that Brazeau coal moves to that point in the eastern direction?

I have not the figures, but I think I can get them.

One of the big questions in the handling of the western railway problem is that as to the distance from existing lines that new lines shall be built. I am not referring now to lines of different systems but to our own lines. I do not know that there is any real reason why the same consideration should not apply to other lines. What policy is being laid down by the directors as to the minimum distance for the construction of new lines for the purpose of giving the farmers service?

In every memorandum I have read to-day in regard to stations the saving that would be made by the construction of the line in mile haulage has been given. In some cases it is twelve miles, in some cases less and in some cases considerably more. The conditions of the locality would have something to do surely with the length of haulage that would be considered a proper haulage, which would not deprive the producer of all profit that the property could make on account of the expense in hauling. I could not give my hon. friend the absolute data as to what ought to be the mileage because I do not know. In some districts where there were good roads the mileage could be longer and still be more profitable than in sections where the roads were bad, where there was a shorter haulage. I pointed out that in all the statements made to-day where grain growing and the question of haulage was being dealt with, the mileage from the producer to the railway was given, and the saving that would be effected by the building of the line under consideration.
I do not think the hon. minister is quite right in that statement. I do not know what is meant by the figures he gives. They just show the haul to the station-

The statement shows the saving.

CJf.R.-Branch Lines

No. In one
sense it does, and in another it does not. It shows the distance at the present time and the distance if the new line were built. But I was asking a different question. I was asking him what, in the opinion of the board, was the minimum distance for the construction of new lines for the purpose of giving the farmers service. We have to get down to some basic principle in this matter unless we are going to have political lines built here and there without any idea of anything except political profit. I would like to know the economic minimum distance in an agricultural district that railways can afford to be placed the one from the other. This is a matter which is absolutely at the foundation of any proper construction of prairie lines. Surely my hon. friend will have some idea on that question of policy.

I will reiterate to a
large extent what I have said. What would be a proper haulage with an idea of profit in one section would be altogether wrong in another section. For example, I might refer to some of the trails over which I have travelled in the West, and which were absolutely good roads. Fifty miles from there a man might have a 12 or 15 mile haul over a bad road. My judgment is based . on inherent knowledge, the same as my hon. friend's judgment. Perhaps fifty miles from that same locality, where the roads are almost impassable, the haulage will have to :be shortened, to be comparable with the haulage in the other districts. I do not pretend to be an expert on this, but I should say when a farmer has to haul his grain more than 10 miles to the railway he is at a disadvantage.

He is always at a disadvantage unless he is located very close to the line. Does the hon. minister think that Sir Henry Thornton and his board can possibly arrange their scheme of prairie branch lines on the basis of a ten mile haul that would give anything like fair play to the country as a whole? Does he know how many branch lines that would mean at the present time? We know these lines are urgently needed in places where people have to haul twenty and thirty miles.
I think it would take very many years for us to complete railway accommodation that would reduce the haul to ten or twelve miles.

The minister
spoke of ten miles a moment ago.

Call it ten. My hon.
friend can call it whatever he likes.

The minister
said ten.

I said ten miles and I will adhere to that. Unless construction is begun to reduce the distance of haulage the producers will never reach what is even approximately a fair haul. If we said we were not prepared to do anything because we could not give everybody a ten mile haul and left them all with a fifty mile haul, it would not be good for the country or the railways. We never can make the Canadian National Railways a success, leaving the producers out of consideration altogether, unless we are prepared to build branch lines as rapidly as we can, in order to converge the traffic to the main line of the Canadian National or to some of its lines. It cannot be all done at once. The present state of our development was not reached in a few years. It is many years ago since the Grand Trunk was built; it had its difficulties, and continued to have them. Then the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed, but at that time there Was not much discussion as to the length of haulage and the amount of traffic. Now we all know that its construction was one of the saviours of Canada. My idea is that while ideals are worth striving for, yet if we are to be pinned down to details as to what the ideal situation should be we will never make a start because such ideals, never can be attained. It will take many years and a much more numerous population than we have to-day to bring about a state of affairs where the haul from the producer to the railway track will approximate the mileage that I have named. However, in many parts of the Dominion that desirable state of affairs does already exist, and I suppose that in the older part of Ontario the haul is hot over ten or twelve miles. I feel that we ought to be generous, if we are to benefit by the experience of our forefathers. They worked hard in order that we -might reach our present state of development. We have fairly good railway facilities in this province, and until the whole Dominion is equally well served', not only will there be -few settlers-for they will not come unless we encourage them-but many of those already here will be likely to move out.

I have been
very much interested and amused but not enlightened by my hon. friend's argument. In effect, he says that if we make ten miles the standard we will do nothing at all. I would think that looking back at our railway history -which m.ust be extremely familiar to my hon. friend-the railway mess made in Ontario
C .N .R .-Branch Lines

under his government would convince him that it was worth while before undertaking further railway construction, to determine what the economic distance between line and line ought to be. It is true that we have many miles of lines in Ontario

lines that we will be paying for for many years to come-where we do not need them, and where, at the present time, the Canadian National Railway Board is taking up rails and disposing of right of way which cost this country millions of dollars. And why? Just because that simple little question, what is the economic necessity, was not first considered. But apparently a bad habit is very hard to eradicate.
Now, I have found when discussing this question with farmers throughout the West- and if my hon. friend does not know anything about it I am going to tell him my own experience-that they recognise-whether my hon. friend does or does not-that it is practically impossible to lay out railways on the basis of a maximum ten mile haul; and, further, that if it were done, in the great majority of cases you would have the whole country gridironed with railways, none of which could possibly pay. I found the farmer of the Northwest possessed quite enough sense to appreciate what would be the probable result. I have also found in most places- and when I was on the railway board I took evidence time and again as to these costs- in an endeavour to co-operate with the local people, because after all the cost ultimately falls on the farmer, I found pretty general agreement with the view that if we could arrange to build our branch railways so that the maximum haul would not exceed fifteen miles it would be all right. Many farmers have told me that mileage has to be considered having regard to. each particular district, but that after all what really counted was whether you could draw your produce to the railway and get back again the same day; this they found they could always do if the haul did not exceed fifteen miles.
If my hon. friend really is sincere in wanting these branches constructed, why does he not furnish us with real business information? Why should there be any difficulty whatever if the board in dealing with it as a matter of business said: "There are just so many land sections between railways built at a given distance apart. In our view the closest distance is so-and-so, and we ought to try and give the people the best service possible, bearing in mind that limitation." Is that an unreasonable suggestion? Is it not something which in the first instance goes directly to the 
consideration of th. whole subject? I would think so.
I would point out to my hon. friend that the next line proposed opens up the same territory. I think the committee ought to have information as to what is to be done with these two lines. There is an extension within a few townships into this section. Is the Lovema line to be carried through to the main line? If so, to what point on the main line? And if it is carried through, what justification is there for the construction of the other line?
Carried.

The hon. member for Pontiac says "carried." On what ground does he suggest that it is carried? Perhaps he would like to assist the committee. The minister himself has suggested that we call it six o'clock and that the committee rise, because he has not the information at present. Perhaps the hon. member for Pontiac has that information and is aching to unburden himself.

My hon. friend has himself already given all the information which any hon. gentleman might want.

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES

speechtext: The House again in committee on the fol-lbwing proposed resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from Hanna to Warden in the province of Alberta: estimated mileage including existing grading, 57 miles: estimated cost, $1,445,000.
Sir HENR\ DRAYTON: We were trying to find out whether any general plan had been adopted as to the economical point at which further railways could be constructed, to see whether the board had considered economies at all in connection with their

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
proposals. If they did look at the matter from that point of view, what do they regard as duplication, what as paralleling, and what the reverse?

I think when my hon.
friend was chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners he stated that as a matter of general policy there should be fifteen miles between railway lines.
Thirty milesa fifteen mile haul.

Well, I think my hon.
friend is wrong about that, speaking offhand, but we can discuss that on any railway bill. With the lines thirty miles apart, to have a fifteen mile haul would mean that there would be a station opposite every farm, otherwise the farmer would have to haul east or west several miles in addition to his haul towards the railway line. If the lines were fifteen miles apart the average haul, I should think, would be ten or twelve miles. I am inclined to think my hon. friend did not put it at thirty miles, because that might mean , more than a thirty mile haul, according to the territory.

My hon.
friend is quite right. You can always find places where it will be a little more or a little less. It is not very hard to get stations-

Try the
Railway Commission and see if it is easy.

Of course, it
costs a great deal more to look after stations and railways than it did. I am speaking of a time when conditions were perhaps some-.what different to those at present prevailing. I do not know exactly what it is like now, but I do know that the general underlying idea was-and of course stations had to be taken into account in that idea-if you have two lines only ten miles apart and no station within ten miles of either side somebody has to haul grain fifteen miles. When you talk about a maximum fifteen mile haul you are not talking about facts. Apart from refinements, and it is not necessary to do very much refining when apparently nothing is done at all, I wonder if any hon. gentleman in this chamber really thinks it is safe to go on building right and left without the slightest idea of what you are going to do with the line when it is built. Do not hon. members think that there should be some determining policy? You have to have stations here and there, but do you not think there should be some determining principle
which would say that lines are not going to be built any more in Canada just for the fun of building them? We expect now that lines shall be built in such a way that they will return a revenue. The prairie country is pretty similar as a rule; the prairie country is pretty extensive, and it needs branch line accommodation more than any part of Canada that I know of. It lends itself more to railway construction than any other part of Canada I know of at the present time, but when you say all that, you have not said an awful lot. You are just recognizing the fact, and you have your limitations. You have your first limitation as to moneys available for railroads; your second limitation as to returns from railroads. I do not suppose anybody in this House wants lines built in the Northwest to-day that are not going to pay. If there are any there ought not to be. I do not suppose there is any gentleman in this House who wants one set of settlers to have lines within ten miles of each other, costing a tremendous lot of money, when other settlers, unless conditions have changed very much since I was on the Railway Commission, because I have been over the ground, are not fifteen miles but thirty or forty miles from the railway. Surely what ought to be done is to try and do justice to everybody to the full extent possible and in order to do that we have to arrive at some reasonable policy.

I agree largely.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Graham thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 44, respecting the construction of a Canadian National Railway line between Hanna and Warden, in the province of Alberta.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from Loverna, in a generally westerly direction, to a point in township 32 or 33, range 9, west of the 4th meridian, in the province of Alberta; estimated mileage including existing grading, 50 miles; estimated cost, $1,192,000.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

What is the
memorandum on that?

The line runs through a good district susceptible of wheat raising and mixed farming, and there is already considerable settlement and development in this area.
The justification for the construction of this line is that it is estimated that 1,500,000 bushels of grain will be produced off it annually, besides 305 cars of in and outbound freight, consisting of live stock, coal, lumber and merchandise. On the average, 16 miles road haul will be saved to the farmers, and this taken at f cents per bushel per mile hauled, on the 1,500,000 bushels estimated to be produced, would be a saving to them of $180,000 per year on grain haul alone.
How do you get at that saving on the farmers' haul of sixteen miles? I would be very interested to learn how that conclusion is arrived at.

That is the statement
given me by the engineers of the road. They figure it at | cents per bushel. I imagine in some cases it would be much more than that.
Do the engineers always take the maximum distance and apply that as the average?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would not apply in this case because this line runs directly between the Canadian Pacific railway and the Goose Lake line of the Canadian National. It is an extension of the Grand Trunk Pacific line from Biggar, which ends at Loverna on the boundary line between Alberta and Saskatchewan. This is a projection between the two lines approximately twenty miles from either.
Is the minister sure it is twenty miles from both?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Approximately. I know the settlement very well.

I would have
thought it would have been a good deal nearer than that. At any rate I think the minister is right, that what they have done is to take the maximum in arriving at their average, and he defends that course because the line is put down the centre. That may be right. It may be a good reason. It may be based on good engineering but it is certainly a novel one. It is proper to ask

how many more transactions of the same kind have happened? I will ask another question. We have had the amount of grain to be hauled. I want to know how much of that is new grain, and how much is grain already produced and handled on the line?
