speechtext: They have been growing grain in that locality for the past fifteen years.
I know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not a
nice piece of country to haul over because it is cut up by creeks. Many farmers have left the locality notwithstanding the fact that they have raised very large crops. The estimate of three-quarters of a cent per bushel for haulage is a very low estimate.

The minister
has not answered the question I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What was
the question?

I thought it
was pretty plain. Is the quantity of grain , under consideration here the quantity that is now produced or does it merely cover the amount that will be produced? That is all I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly, when the railway goes in the amount of grain produced will be doubled. I may tell my hon. friend that the district has been settled for the past fifteen years. Furthermore, settlement went into the locality because of the stakes that were there, as it has gone into many other localities, and the people have patiently waited all these years for railway construction.
I have not got an answer to the question yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Grain is
grown there. It has been grown for more than fifteen years. Is that the information my hon. friend wanted?

No. We have
had an amount of grain stated. Is that the amount which will be produced?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One million bushels? I should say four or five million bushels. Let me say to my hon. friend that one station in a territory where grain is being grown will produce one million bushels itself.

Then that statement is entirely incorrect.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it
is very conservative.

May I say to the minister that I believe the estimate with regard to the number of bushels that will be produced in this territory is entirely too low.
I know the remarks of the Minister of the Interior are prompted by a knowledge of the conditions out there, a knowledge which I think the ex-Minister of Finance lacks. For example in my constituency one place, the town of Gleichen, shipped this year a million bushels. The town of Vulcan shipped two million bushels, and there are many points, especially in this portion of the province from which that amount was shipped. That production could undoubtedly be doubled if conditions were created that would keep the farmers in that part of the country. The want of population is largely attributable to lack of transportation facilities. That want will continue until the lack is supplied. The resolution provides for the construction of a line running from Loverna in a generally westerly direction. Would the minister have any objection to informing the committee just where the destination of the line is to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The original destination of this line, as my hon. friend knows, was Calgary and the original idea was that it should be a Grand Trunk Pacific branch line. Since the amalgamation of these roads, Hanna would be the terminus of this project.

That is what I was afraid of. I register as powerful a protest as I am capable of against Hanna being used as the terminus for this branch line. There is an enormous territory north of Hanna which is suffering for want of transportation, I mean the country round Dowling lake, Long lake and so on. It is well settled, the land is excellent for agricultural purposes. The settlement went in there under the promise and expectation that this line would be built, and built long before now. If this line runs down to Hanna, and you have the other side of the triangle running from Hanna to Warden, you will have an enormous triangular area south of the Canadian Pacific the centre part of which will be 25 miles or more from the railway itself. That can be entirely eliminated by continuing the line westerly and meeting the Hanna and Warden line, at a point 20 miles south of Warden, or if the engineers considered it advisable running into Big Valley. I am sorry there is no 74
map on an adequate scale in the chamber so that I could point out the situation to members of the committee. However if they look at one carefully they will realize the practicability of the scheme as I am outlining it. I understood last year from the management of the Canadian National Railways that it was their intention to run this line from Loverna to a point about 20 miles southeast of Warden. That is all right. If it is decided to go to Warden that is the logical end of the line. But to run the line to Hanna would be perfectly absurd. It would leave the greater part of that territory still unsupplied with transportation facilities, and I protest against any such action.

As far as this line goes I think it ought to be built. I must say that I base my conclusion more on facts within my own knowledge, than on any facts supplied by the minister from the directorate. Indeed I am convinced from the whole material presented by the minister from the directorate that the latter know very little about any of these lines, and I think hon. members who are supporting them are doing so more on the basis of their own knowledge than on any information supplied them in this way. It is said that 1,500,000 bushels of grain will be produced and delivered to this line. Well, it is obvious that there ought to be three or four times that amount -five times possibly and four times anyway -produced. I have not the least doubt there would be. But 1,500,000 bushels is the amount given us in this information. Then the statement goes on to say that the hauling of this grain, estimated at three-quarters of a cent per bushel, would save on the average of sixteen miles of road haul, therefore saving the farmers $180,000. You really could not have greater humbug than that. As to the haulage the average man would save, sixteen miles would be the maximum saving for anyone. A few might save a little more but it is obvious, by looking at the map, that there would be ten per cent save sixteen miles, and the other ninety per cent would save anywhere from sixteen miles down to one mile. How anyone can suggest that the average farmer would save a sixteen mile haul and state it seriously, is something I cannot understand. As represented to me, not by one but by many, because of the far greater amount of grain that will be produced than is stated here, the average saving in the hauling applied to all that grain, say of eight or nine miles, would represent the amount stated here. I

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

only call attention to this matter to show how utterly unreliable this data is. This has been supplied, I suppose, by some engineer, certainly not by any practical man.
Oh, oh.

Certainly not a practical man for deciding how much grain is going to be delivered to a railway, and how -much is going to be saved in delivering it. If the National Railway is dependent on this kind of data to decide what to do I think parliament will have to apply its own intelligence and apply it very closely. My judgment is that this whole programme is not really based on the opinion of the National Railway directors at all. It is based on representations that h#ve been made to the government from the district, and I venture to say mostly representations by members of parliament. They have taken it up with the directors, and after the whole thing is through the directors have come to a compromise with them, and so it goes. Consequently, we are really called upon, in respect of every single line, to bring to bear our own information and local knowledge, and without that we would be pretty much in the dark. I hope that later on some means can be taken to lay more directly before each and every member who has not the advantage of local knowledge some statement of the situation, because as we stand to-day it really is not fair to hon. members to call upon them to support this proposition. The facts are not before them.

I do not want to raise
any controversy at the present time over the general practice in regard to information given by the government when asking for a grant of money to build branch lines. I submit this statement, however, with unqualified confidence: that a greater amount of information has been given on each one of these lines than was given in regard to the branch lines project in 1920.
The minister was not in the House.
This is one of the times when, fortunately, Hansard talks, but I do not want to raise the question now because I want to get the resolutions through and build these lines.

My point is that the
information given is not dependable.

Then my hon. friend
would say that no information at all would be better.

Yes, rather than this
information.
That would be the only defence they could have for the procedure in 1920 because they gave no information whatever.
They gave all that was asked.

I will show it to my hon. friend. Here is the branch line programme. It was in the estimates but not so stated. I mean that the lines were not in the general estimates, if my information is correct. There was a great deal of discussion. I was not present, but at page 4232 of Hansard of June 25th, 1920, there is considerable discussion about the branch lines. One hon. member says he is only going to discuss the Hudson Bay railway, and another hon. member wants some information as to the Humboldt-Melfort branch, and the reply of the minister, Mr. Reid, was:
I can give a list of the lines I have here. The Humboldt-Melfort has a grade of 5.4 and a 32 track.
Then Mr. Campbell asks:
Will that complete the line between Humboldt and Melfort entirely?
And the minister replies:
I understand it will.
Then the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) asks this question:
I think that if the minister would give us the details of the whole of these lines it would be more instructive to hon. members. The statement could appear on Hansard.
Then follows the information with a list of the lines:
Line	Work to be done 1920
Line now under construction _ Grade Track
Then we find a statement of the different lines and the grade and track. There may be some information somewhere else. I have not been able to find it. The statement of the minister here gives the amount of grading to be done and the amount of track. As far as I can find out, it does not give the terminus or the starting point, but that will be in some particular some place else. The cost of some of these lines is not in this list at all. This list just gives the mileage and there is absolutely no information in it.

The practice was to lay on the Table detailed data which did not appear in Hansard, because it was laid on the Table, but it was available for every member. Information was never denied. It will be re-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
called also that in those cases the money was voted separately in the estimates, and debates took place as well.
This is when the estimates were up.
Yes.
No resolution, because they were in the estimates.

A great many of us who are in the House to-day were not here in 1920, and if the opposition of that day did not see fit to get the proper information they simply were not doing their duty by the country.
Was the government doing their duty by not furnishing the information?

I am relying on the statement of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who says the data was laid on the Table. Apparently it was not inspected by the opposition of that day. The opposition did not deem it necessary in the country's interest to make a study of the data, and consequently the Branch Lines Bills, I suppose, went through without any particular study by the then opposition. But to-day we have a different opposition, and so far as this particular member of the opposition is concerned, I propose at least to oppose these branch lines until we get data which is reliable and accurate. All any hon. member has to do is to go to the Table and look at the map and he will see that an absolute misrepresentation has been made by the engineer. I do not connect the minister with it, because he is simply reading the report of the engineer; but any engineer who cannot make measurements on a map to scale should not be in the employ of the Canadian National. As far as I can see, you cannot find any point along the line of that railway, if the railway is fifty miles long, where the distance would be fifteen miles from the railway, and yet the engineer says that the average distance that any farmer will save in haul will be sixteen miles. The thing is absolutely ridiculous, and I am astonished that an engineer should think he could put it over in that way.
That may mean eight miles coming and eight miles going.
Even taking it in that way, coming and going it would be impossible.

speechtext:
I do not

When the

Mr. Chairman, I am
quite familiar with the country through which this railroad would be constructed. There seems to be some controversy as to how far men are hauling their wheat there to-day. 
A glance at the map will show that we do not have stations at every crossroads in that country. After a man strikes the railroad1 he has to go down five miles to the nearest station to unload his wheat. His haul is from his home to the nearest elevator, and as the elevators are ten miles apart his haul cannot be estimated by figuring it from a certain point to the nearest railroad. I know that people went into that country fifteen years ago expecting this railroad to be built. It is an excellent farming country, and not only will this road be called upon to haul out wheat but to bring in coal from the Drum-heller district to supply the country from Loverna to Biggar. That coal now comes by a roundabout route. This line will put Us eventually in direct connection with the coal fields, and the freight will be an exceedingly important source of income. Certainly, the road should be built. It seems to me that it is good sensible economy to build it now, because otherwise the people cannot stay there much longer. Many have already gone out, but they will come back if railway facilities are' provided. The country is capable of producing far more wheat than is shown by the estimate, and will furnish an abundance of traffic. I think the road should be built, and built now.

I want to try to make
clear to the minister-I really think it is clear to everybody else-what I was arguing before. He allowed his anger to get the better of him, and his arithmetic retrogressed as his anger increased. First of all, I would explain that I am not opposing the road.
That is better.

What does the hon.
member say?

That is better. It is
not what we understood when he started.
I am sorry. I know the hon. member understands English very well, and I have said that three times before.

The hon. gentleman
has such a peculiar way of surrounding everything he says that we do not know on what foot he stands.

I do not catch my hon.
friend's remark, but he evidently would like to escape this question of addition. What the engineer says, and bases his whole calculation on, is that the average road haul will, after this road is built, be sixteen miles less than it was before. Now, I stated that patently that was nonsense. The minister does not seem to see that the saving in the

average road haul must be the difference between the average road haul before and what it will be after the railway is built. He put the latter road haul at eight miles. I do not think he is very far out, but if anything, he is low. So the average road haul before must have been twenty-four miles. But admittedly twenty-four miles is the maximum. Therefore, his figures are simply foolish; that is all. I do not say that the estimates will not be borne out, but that is merely because he made as big an error one way in being too low as he made the other way in being too high. The other error is that the estimate of the grain to be grown is far too low. I venture to say there is more grain grown now. I hope I have made clear to the minister that whoever this engineer is he has disclosed such errore that we cannot depend on his calculations at all. I am not
going to quarrel with my hon. friend about averages.

Mr. Chairman, continuing the protest I made to the minister-to which he has paid no attention whatever-may I read to him from the memorandum of an association that was organized in the winter of 1921 throughout all the municipalities east of Big Valley, a territory which is entirely ignored, according to the Minister of the Interior, in the completion of this line? The association so organized became active in 1922 for the following purposes:
To draw the attention of the government to the fact:
1.	That the settlers within this area have waited over twelve years since the first survey was made.
2.	That the area described is well and extremely productive as shown by the last census returns.
3.	That this extension would assist in the development of two coal fields of exceptional promise.
The association advised the farmers to assist the government in building the road, and I simply wish to quote their figures to indicate to the House their deadly earnestness. They made the suggestion, and bound themselves by agreement, to offer to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, if the company would only permit them to build the road, a bonus on a sliding scale as follows:
Each man who lived from one to two miles distant from the railroad would pay $60 per quarter section, from two to three miles distant, $50 per quarter section; from three to four miles distant, $40 per quarter section; from four to five miles distant, $30 per quarter section; from five to six miles distant, $20 per quarter section, and from six to seven miles distant, $10 per quarter section.
This shows how far these men were willing to go in helping to build the line and how anxious they were to see it undertaken. That offer was rejected; why, I do not understand. But may I say to hon. members that the financial ability of those men to-day to renew that promise is gone, but the spirit which then animated them is still there. But they will not and cannot stay in that territory if the line to Big Valley is not put through. Therefore, I should like an assurance from the minister that he will take up the matter earnestly with the management and have the line completed.

I apologise to the hon.
member for neglecting him, but only one speaker can have the floor at a time, and I have not had a chance, this question of averages having got away beyond me. I am glad to get back to the railway. I understand that the point at which the line suggested is to join the other line has not yet been determined, which allows full opportunity for representations to be made to the board. Formerly, these were competing lines. To-day, the management is trying to co-ordinate and use all the lines to the fullest advantage and so secure as direct a route as possible. I will certainly bring to the attention of the board what my hon. friend has said, and I think I may safqly tell him that up to date it has not been decided at what point on that line the connection will be made.
I was simply going on the suggestion of the Minister of Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) that he thought that Hanna was to be the terminal point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That assertion is based on the fact that the line is following identically the old survey. I know the situation as outlined by my hon. friend and undoubtedly the settlement of Dowling Lake is important.

The Minister of the Interior knows enough about the situation to be able to endorse everything that I have said. I see he nods his head, and I am glad to have his approval. It is quite true that the original survey did run to Hanna but since that time there have been three other surveys, one north of Drumheller between Rowley and Morrin, another running into Big Valley, and now, as I understand, a fourth running into Warden. It is clear therefore that there are contemplated a number of surveys, and I sincerely trust that Hanna will not be the one that will be followed.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

I can support all that
has 'been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Garland, Bow River). I think the Minister of the Interior will remember that when he was Premier of the province of Alberta I headed a deputation requesting his government to allow the people to tax themselves for the purpose of assisting this particular branch line when it was under the jurisdiction of the Grand Trunk Railway. The area to be served is very well populated and has been considerably developed. I took a trip through the district last fall and I am sorry to say that I discovered that many of the settlers had left because they had no railway communication at hand. In discussing this matter with the people in that particular district I was informed by many of them that during the fall they had to make trips to the Canadian Pacific Railway on the north at a cost of from $8 to $16 a trip to carry a load of grain.
How many bushels?

About 120. You can
understand that under these circumstances it is impossible for these people to remain in that locality very much longer unless they get this branch line, and get it at the earliest opportunity. These people have been very patient and have made many pilgrimages to Winnipeg to induce the officials to build this branch line; and knowing the district as I do I am satisfied that this particular piece of railway will be a very profitable one. There is available annually a quantity from four to six million bushels of wheat throughout this [DOT]territory, and naturally there would also be other freight in addition to grain. As regards the terminus of this particular branch, I suggest very respectfully to the minister that in discussing the matter with the board he decide not to run into Hanna. In my opinion the line should be kept further north in order to afford the people in that part of the country the accommodation which they so badly require.

When does the minister
expect to have the detailed information regarding this line and others as well?

I think I can safely say that the information which I have been giving to the House in connection with these resolutions is somewhat more detailed than I can recollect having been given to parliament before. Of course, I need not say that I want to give to hon. members all the information that is available; there is nothing to hide but rather everything to gain in so doing. I might suggest that the information I am giv-
ing is rather modest in that the grain that will be available in these districts, it is suggested, is about three times as much as the railways have estimated.
I think it has been clearly indicated that the information which the minister has given us is so inaccurate as not to be accepted.

Not at all; on what point is it inaccurate?
Mr. CLx\RK:	On the question of average
distances.

Let me answer that
point.
If I may resume afterwards.

Certainly. Some hon. members who have not listened carefully to the statements that I have made have jumped at the conclusion that the engineers reported that the saving in the distance would be so many miles. That is not what the engineers have said, nor is it what I have read. If one is figuring a rate, say, on coal from Alberta some provision must be made for getting the empty cars back. So that the rates are based not altogether on what it takes to move a certain quantity from one point to another; if that were all, then the provisions for traffic would run out in a short time. The vehicles have to be brought back to the point of shipment and therefore allowance must be made therefor. Some hon. gentlemen laughed when one hon. member said that the men with the teams had to drive back eight miles; and what I am pointing out to the committee is that if there were nothing for the farmer to take back the cost of the haulage of his grain must include the trip going as well as coming.

In some of the other cases it certainly was not figured on any such basis. Will the minister tell the committee that in some of the other cases we have dealt with the engineers were taking into account the haul both going and coming?
I am not referring to cost; my hon. friend's reference to that question is entirely beside the mark and he knows it. What I am referring to is the length of the road haul upon which the engineer is basing his calculations; and I want the minister to state on his responsibility what is meant in the reports when the road haul is mentioned. Is it to the station and back, or simply to the station?

I cannot say what was in the engineer's mind.

I know you cannot.
If I were figuring the cost of hauling I would figure both ways, including the empty conveyance going as well as the full load. And any sane man would do the same.
Does the estimate of three quarters of a cent per bushel per mile apply to the 8 miles or the 16 miles? In other words, is it going or coming, or both?

I have stated the case as clearly as I can. The ex-Minister
9.	p.m. of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) said that it had nothing to do with the question of cost, while my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) says that it has.
I am not saying anything.
I stated a moment ago exactly what the case was, no matter what the engineers may have had in mind; and that is, that the cost of haulage would include going as well as coming.

We might as well try to be fair with each other in this matter. There is a question of cost which is based on length of haul. There is cost coming and going, there is no dispute about that, and when you come to count your cost coming and going you would have a right to some allowance at both ends, unless, as the Minister of Interior, I think, said, you are getting something back in a return haul. But that has to do only with distance. It may be that the hon. gentleman is quite right if he wants to double costs for the haul. But I want to see whether as a matter of fact we can rely upon anything in connection with these estimates. When it is said that the haul to the railway is a given number of miles, does that mean distance or does it mean return journey? Which way are we to read these reports? Surely my hon. friend understands that. Surely that is something we ought to know. The ordinary acceptance of the term is that distance is distance and does not cover return mileage. Unless we know how to read these reports we cannot give any intelligent consideration to the matter. Are we to have a different reaffing for every single report, according to the exigencies of the case?

I want to read the statement the minister made with regard to the road haul. Whether there has been an attempt to do it or not, I think the members are confused as to just what the saving will be. I have examined the map which is on the table and so far as I can judge the maximum haul
would be about seventeen miles, and the average would be very much less-not more, I should think, than six or seven miles. Now, this is what the statement says that the minister read to the committee:
On the average, sixteen miles road haul will be saved to the farmers,-
That might be taken the way the minister interprets it, if it stopped there; it might be both ways, eight miles going and eight miles coming. But taken with what follows I say his interpretation is an impossible one. What follows is this:
-and this taken at |c per bushel per mile hauled-
So that it reads as follows:
On the average, sixteen miles road haul will be saved to the farmers, and this taken at |c per bushel per mile hauled-
That means the number of miles you haul the number of bushels you have on your wagon; it cannot mean anything else. Any other interpretation, I contend, is simply ridiculous.
Do you think you do not have to haul the wagon back?

Absolutely, but you do not
haul the grain both ways, and that is what this statement says. The reference is to the bushels that are being hauled, not to the return of the empty wagon. It is as clear as the English language can make it. If the committee is to be properly informed about these branch lines we must have before us those* who know something about the matter. I would like to know whether the minister has seen the profiles or the plans for these railways.

Why should he see them?
1 do not build railways. I am not a railway builder.

There you are. I would
like to see the plans and profiles. I would like to see what the grades are like, for instance. If I could see the profiles and had a report on the surrounding country I would have some idea, ignorant though I am on railway building, whether it was feasible to put a railway into this country. It is true that it is easy to build railways in the prairie country, but we have other country besides prairie country. I know of areas on the prairie into which I think even hon. gentlemen on my left would not be enthusiastic about building a railway. We have all seen country on the prairies where none of us would want to put a railway if it were not for the fact that we have to go through it.	[DOT]

I cannot hear my hon. friend, but from what I make of his question I do not think it has anything to do with what I am discussing. If my hon. friend wants a discussion on that perhaps he can get some of his fellow members to go outside and talk about it. I am trying to stick to the question now before the committee, which has reference to these particular branch lines. As I say, I think the only feasible and sensible thing to do is to bring down the plans and profiles and have these engineers appear before a committee-these engineers who so obviously, to my mind, make incorrect statements, as shown by the map the minister has placed on the Table. If we could get into committee with the plans and profiles before us, with decent maps, with witnesses who know the country and who can tell us whether these things are necessary, it might be plain sailing, and perhaps we could support all these proposals. As it stands now I cannot see how I can support any of them unless I happen to know personally the country that the particular line goes through, and I think if members are honest with themselves they must come to the same conclusion. I do not see how they can support a proposal to expend millions of dollars for a line of railway they know nothing about.

It has been settled during alii that period and I know of my own knowledge of at least six who left that territory and abandoned a section five years ago because they were unable to make a livelihood on account of the long haul which they had to make of their produce to market. I am astonished at the statement made by the Minister of the Interior.

I think I have stated what
I wished to say to the minister and to this House. I cast no reflection on the word of any hon. member. But we find the ministers know nothing about it; they give us information which is wrong, as is shown by the map, and they have to be corrected by members over here; then they ask us to accept the explanation given by the members for the constituencies concerned. I say that is most unsatisfactory. The only way we can get down to business and get the facts is by bringing the engineers, and if necessary the president of the road, and his directors if they know anything about it, which I doubt very much, before the committee so that we can find out whether the information the minister is giving us is correct or whether the information given by the members representing the constituencies through which these lines run is correct.

Possibly I
can assist, my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) with regard to this rate per bushel business. The custom in that country when a man is hired to haul grain is not to ask him how much he will haul it for per mile, but to ask him how much he wants to haul the grain say seven miles, and the man who is undertaking to haul the grain always takes into consideration the two-way haul, not simply the oneway haul. I am afraid my hon. friend has not lived in that part of the country long enough to understand either the conditions there or the practice in connection with contracts for grain hauling.

I think perhaps we have asked for all the information that is worth while asking for. We have certainly not got the information we have asked for.
I suppose in closing it is due the House that we should thank the hon. Minister of the Interior for his quiet, kindly and temperate remarks, and for that great grip of the business side of railroads that he has displayed.
I am quite sure that everybody who is at all interested in the question of returns from the National roads will feel a tremendous relief when he learns that simply because the hon. member for Burrard is charged with making a speech in one part of the country which he did not make, this line is a perfectly good line to build.

Provided that for the purpose of avoiding duplication-
I want to direct the minister's attention to the wording of this statute:
Provided that for the purpose of avoiding duplication of construction of that portion of the line west of Lloydminster, the approval of the route map may be made subject to joint construction or operation with the Canadian Northern Railway Company, on terms to be agreed upon by the companies or settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
I think the minister made a slight reference to that in his opening remarks, if I caught him correctly. Will the minister be good enough to explain to the committee how much of this Canadian Pacific line has been constructed as authorized by this statute, between Edmonton and Lloydmin-
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

ster? I agree with the hon. member for Rattleford (Mr. McConica) that the territory through which this line is projected is certainly good producing territory; and furthermore I would! judge, both from a study of the map before me and also from my recollection of the discussion in the Railway committee room five years ago, that it is a very desirable thing that that territory should be served, but I want to point out that it is wholly undesirable that there shall be a duplication of roads through that district.
Now a moment's reflection will bring to the attention of the House that there is a paralleling of lines from Saskatoon west. There is perhaps a couple of hundred miles at least where two and sometimes three lines are running almost within sight of one another-a most deplorable situation. There is no reason in the world why, under the present conditions of stringency and desire for economy, the Canadian National Railways should enter into an undertaking which may result in serious duplication, or should undertake the construction of a road through a territory which is being served partially, and perhaps as time proceeds, more rapidly by the other system than the government can serve it by the system which they propose to put in. I know the usual answer to an argument of this kind is that the member is looking after the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That is not the case. '
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear." He may take what pleasure he likes out of it; but we are brought down to this point, that hon. members might take seriously the fact that the time has passed when we in Canada can go on duplicating the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other railway; and it is not going to deter me one iota in making these assertions or pointing out the facts, if some hon. member says "hear, hear," to the suggestion that an hon. member is speaking for the Canadian Pacific Railway when he is uttering these sentiments. Certainly it is in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway, if you like, that the other railway shall not be allowed to duplicate it, but it is infinitely more in the interests of the country, that we shall not duplicate these lines any longer. Furthermore, any proposition that has in contemplation the construction of a line through a territory occupied by another railway is improvident and unwise at this time.
I desire to say to the minister in connection practically with all the fines at this time-it has been in my mind to say it during all these 
discussions-that the minister comes before parliament with twenty-six railway bills. We are told that the railways are divorced from politics, and that the desire of the minister and the government is that the National Railways shall be kept as distinct and apart from political interference as possible. Let us give the minister full credit for that statement, and for the best intentions in that regard. Then why cannot this corporate body, the National Railway Company-for it is a corporate body- come before parliament and the committee, just the same as any corporate body does? Is there any objection to that?

The hon. member might permit me to answer that question now because I might forget it. The other companies to which he refers supply their own money. Parliament has to supply the money in this case; consequently at this stage parliament has to be approached directly. As a matter of fact we have yet to go through the bill stage with every one of these lines.
The minister will then send it to committee.

I have not said it but I do say it will be impossible to send the resolutions to committee. I say it is impossible; but, of course, parliament can do anything. Practically, it would be absolutely impossible to send parliamentary resolutions to the committee. Of course when bills are introduced it is a different thing; we can send them to committee. The suggestion is worthy of consideration. However under our parliamentary practice we could not send the resolutions to committee, and we require to have resolutions to provide for money before the provision can be embodied in a bill.

The hon. minister has not made a very satisfactory case. He argues in one breath that this National Railway must come to parliament for its money, and, therefore, it should come before parliament for its bill. Ijn the next breath he tells us it is quite possibLe he will send these bills direct to the Railway committee.
I did not quite say that.
Not quite but very near. Will the minister give us his assurance that they will be sen-t to committee?
What would they be sent to committee for?

Will the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) excuse me? I know the hon. member was very near being Minister of Railways, but not quite.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

What would they be sent
there for? Will you answer that?

Will the minister state
that he will send them to the Railway committee-
My hon. friend is insatiable.

He may find me a little
less satiable than I have been if his answers are not satisfactory.

We will not get excited.
I said the time to consider this would be when we got into the bill stage. I think my hon. friend is crowding me hard in asking me to pledge parliament and the Canadian National Railway Board that these bills will be sent to the Railway committee. It is a matter for consideration.

I cannot see any difficulty. If it is a matter of policy to put these bills through this committee and not through the Railway committee, surely it is not difficult for the minister to say so. It is a question whether the minister would allow it, not a question to be conned over by the House. I am very glad the minister answered as he did, for it lays bare the danger of the whole business. The minister says that parliament is the only place to which this railway can come for money. But we are training the directorate to think that they can dip into the treasury whenever they like. Taking at 100 per cent what the minister and the government have been protesting for the past two and a half years, that they want to divorce the National Railway system from politics, I say to them, let the Canadian National Railway Board be treated just the same as the Canadian Pacific Railway Board are treated-let them come before the Railway committee with their bills, and before the Board of Railway Commissioners with their plans and profiles and make their applications. Then there may be some opportunity of checking these things properly. We can judge the policy of the government by the utterances of the ministers. What did the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) say a moment ago? Let me bring it to his attention. When we were discussing the other bill, the minister upbraided my colleague from Burrard (Mr. Clark) because he refused to take the word of certain hon. members. "Oh," he said, "should not we take-"
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend from
Bow River finds a lot of amusement very easily. The minister said, "Oh, should we not take the word of hon. gentlemen opposite about this? We had the evidence"-this is his expression-"of three or four hon. gentlemen regarding this territory." Now I ask the government, is that the attitude they are going to take? I am expressing nothing derogatory of my hon. friends to the left if I say that it is surely not going to be the policy of this House to accept as evidence of need of railway facilities merely the request of the member of parliament representing the constituency affected. Is that to be the basis upon which this House is going to grant millions of dollars for expenditure on branch lines? Have we no right to ask for explanations from the government? Are such expenditures not to be subject to scrutiny?

propose to allow my hon. friend to put words of that kind into my1 mouth.

Where are we drifting
to? Hon. gentlemen come to the House and say that there is need for a certain railway; and the directors of the National system sit back-many of them political appointees, as I will show in a moment-and say, "We want a railway in Antigonish, we

want a railway in Guysborough, we want a railway in New Brunswick, we want a railway here, we want a railway there."
An. hon. MEMBER: And in New Brunswick.

Yes, and in New Brunswick. And all this committee can do in functioning at all is to utter a pious "Amen" to these demands, provided certain members stand in their places and say, "Everything is all right." That is the situation with which we are faced to-day. I protest that the National Railway management should get into the habit of simply relying on the treasury to supply funds for any project that comes into their minds, unless we have an opportunity of scrutinizing their proposals with the care which we in this quarter of the House exercise with the meagre information at our disposal, and also have an opportunity of examining the officials before the Railway committee.
Let me draw attention to the difference in procedure. The minister apparently is not favourable to going before the Railway committee. Now, if we had, for instance, Mr. Ruel-one of the most able railway lawyers in Canada and thoroughly acquainted with all this business, one of the best railway representatives that I have seen before the Railway committee in the last ten or twelve years-if we had him before the committee and the engineers we would be able to find out from them by examination the real merits of these lines, and in case of threatened duplication we could have before us representatives of the Canadian Pacific to find out from them to what extent duplication would be precipitated. We cannot do that to-night. There is no possibility of getting this information. In my estimation every one of these bills ought to go before the Railway committee to be scrutinized. Furthermore, if the minister is going to insist on this system of financing the National Railways, that is, by bringing bills before parliament year after year in this fashion, then the National Railway system ought to be made subject to the Board of Railway Commissioners in so far as duplication and similar matters are concerned, just the same as any other railway is subject to their authority. If this railway system is to be divorced from politics, if it is to be free from the interference and influence of members of parliament, then let it be treated in the same way as the other great railway , system, and there will be more confidence on the part of the people in voting money for this purpose.

I am tempted to make a brief rev.Jw of the Board of Directors of the National Railways in order that we may test the value of the reports that have been brought before the House. I question, and advisedly so, whether Sir Henry Thornton-a gentleman who has won a very high position in the estimation of the public in the short time during which he has been head of the system -I question very much if he to-day would give his approval of many of these branch lines. I am quite certain that he is not nearly so well acquainted with them as perhaps most hon. members imagine him to be.
It is just as well for us shareholders to look our directors over now and again. The minister has described this House as a shareholders' meeting. Well, let me contrast the present directorate with the directorate which was deposed. I am not going to say anything regarding Sir Henry Thornton as compared with Mr. D. B. Hanna. The change has been made, and we are desirous of giving Sir Henry Thornton every conceivable support and assistance in his efforts to make a success of these roads. Mr. Mitchell was removed and Mr. Ruel put in his place. I have no complaints respecting Mr. Ruel. He is one of the best railway lawyers in Canada. That is what he is, a technical, legal adviser; so we can eliminate him from consideration. And Major Graham Bell is a representative of the minister, an old civil servant of standing. But what does Major Bell know about these railways? He was over in France most of the year trying to straighten out the Scribe hotel tangle, and therefore he does not enter into consideration. Mr. Robert Hobson of Hamilton, -who is a gentleman of very high standing, was replaced by Mr. Gough of Home Bank fame, of the city of Toronto. Mr. Gough sat on the board of directors for perhaps a year or more and he has passed out. I do not suppose it will be a happy recollection for the minister that he ever appointed Mr. Gough to the position. However, he has replaced that gentleman with Mr. Macdougall of Brockville.
No, Toronto.
A stockbroker, of Toronto.
A very able man.
A very able man? Well, let us say rather a very loyal partisan; for if he has any public virtue it consists in his loyalty.

He is a very able man
indeed.
Well, no doubt the Godt-bless-you of the hon. member for St. Law-
