renoe-St. George is of some value. Then Mr. E.	R. Wood, one of the ablest financiers in Canada, was removed, but I do not know who replaced him. I do not suppose his successor has been appointed. I might observe in passing that Mr. Wood, who was always a Liberal, was appointed by the previous government; and Mr. R. T. Riley, an equally strong Liberal, was also an appointee of that administration. Mr. Riley was removed am} in his stead we have Mr. Dawson, of Prince Rupert.
Was Mr. Riley appointed prior to 1917 or not?

Now that the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) has projected himself into the debate, I suggest that perhaps we might have a new directorate comprising, among others, the hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou), the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy), the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Ham-mell), with a few others sprinkled in. With such a directorate, including 'Mr. Duncan Marshall and Mr. W. T. R. Preston, we should have a splendid political organization. But, to continue, we have, as I say, Mr. Dawson of Prince Rupert, and it is no wonder that the minister turns his back to me when I mention that gentleman's name, because there is absolutely nothing in Mr. Dawson's private or public record to warrant his appointment as a director of the railways. I say this in a spirit of the utmost kindness towards Mr. Dawson. We have also Mr. Talbot of Quebec, a noted partisan; certainly he is noted for nothing else but his partisanship. And then there is our dear old colleague of many years' standing Mr. Sinclair of Guysborough, the mention of whose name brings to our recollection the pitiful wails which we heard for years with reference to the famous Guysborough railway. So soon as Mr. Sinclair has left the House and got upon the railway board, however, we have a political railway- a political football for twenty years-advocated by this gentleman who for so many years had so much to say in regard to matters of this kind.
You cannot say anything against him.

He is a charming gentleman but so far as his fitness for a position on the directorate of the railways goes, no one who knows him thoroughly would for a moment suggest that he was qualified to offer advice on any question appertaining to railway construction. Now here we have a very excellent political board; and as an equally
excellent corollary to that we have the right of the board at discretion to dip into the treasury and take whatever money they want for the construction of any line. And further than that, we have the opinion of the minister that we should not send these bills to the Railway committee because, forsooth, the money supplied for the railways comes out of the treasury and is not furnished by private parties. If the government is in any sense sincere in its desire to divorce these railways, to which we are giving consideration, from politics, let these bills be sent to the Railway committee and let them stand or fall on their merits before that committee. Personally I have been wholly in favour of many of these lines and I am prepared to support them either in any bill or before the committee. But there are other lines, and this is one of them, that cannot be supported by logic, by reason, in equity, or upon any principles of economy.

My hon. friend seems to have a short memory. It was either in 1918 or 1919 that the government of which he was a distinguished member, in the dying days of its career, passed through this House a bill which deprived the Railway committee of all discretion in the matter of branch lines in connection with the Canadian National Railways. That government, if I remember rightly, passed through the House by closure a bill covering 44 branch lines, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) will no doubt recall the circumstance. When we on this side of the House were then sitting opposite we insisted on having the branch lines go before the Railway committee to decide whether they should be granted extensions of time if necessary, and to decide other related questions. My hon. friend points out that the Canadian Pacific Railway asked for a branch line similar to the one now under consideration. I remember that too; but the hon. gentleman must also remember that at that time the Liberal opposition were fighting in this House to have the branch lines submitted to the
10	p.m. Railway committee, and the government of that day opposed the proposal. My hon. friend was then sitting about where I am now, and he among others opposed the submission of the branch lines bills to the Railway committee.
This branch line was before the Railway committee at the same time as the Canadian Pacific Railway branch line.

Every branch line included in this undertaking was before the
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

Railway committee. But instead of sending them back for renewal from year to year, or every second year, my hon. friend's party of that date, then in power, objected, and his leader (Mr. Meighen) who is now sitting in front of him, no doubt remembers the situation. Making a speech, my hon. friend used exactly the same argument as the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) is using tonight, that the money had to come from parliament and that therefore these questions would be reviewed in parliament, so that there was no necessity for sending them to the Railway committee.
The hon. member had better have reference to Hansard. I did not have charge of the Branch Lines Bill, and I have no recollection of the debate in question.
My hon. friend was general utilities man at the time; he had charge of Canadian Northern affairs.
I did not have charge of the Branch Lines Bill and had practically nothing to do with it directly.

If the hon. gentleman will refer to Hansard of that day he will find that he came to the rescue of the Minister of Railways, Dr. Reid, on almost every occasion. When Dr. Reid was asked for information, the stock answer was, not in the public interest; and when we asked for further information my hon. friend usually came to his colleague's assistance. I must say of course that he did so in a very able manner, but he was one of the men who used the argument that it was not necessary to send the matter to the Railway committee. Well, it does not appear to be necessary to send it to the committee at this stage. The purpose of the Railway committee is to grant charters to companies to extend lines into certain territories, and once charters are granted there is nothing further to come before the Railway committee unless you want to do what the opposition of that day advocated, and what the leader of the opposition to-day will not advocate, namely, bring the officials of the railwaj' before members of parliament and question them on all these matters. My hon. friend objected to this course at that time and he has objected to it in this debate in the last few days. But that is the only means of obtaining information at first hand, if that is what we want. The Minister of Railways has furnished the committee with the information that he has obtained from the department. If hon. gentlemen want further information 
and if the leader of the opposition will move for it, I am satisfied that the government will be glad to grant it, because that is the thing we advocated in opposition and the very thing my hon. friends opposite opposed most strongly. Here is a sample of what the then Minister of Railways gave us when he was building branch lines in 1920. I put this question:
I think that if the minister would give us the details of the whole of these lines it would be more instructive to hon. members. The statement could appear on Hansard.
The minister said, "Perhaps I can give the list"; then he goes on; "Alsask, S.E. 16 miles," and so on down the list, covering 312 miles of railway. Not one detail was given as regards expenditure on each of the proposed branch lines. The whole sum was lumped, $48,000,000, and that was all the information the House had at that time. Later on a question was asked of the minister as follows:	\
What work has been done on the Kamloops line up to date?
And here is the answer:
I will try and get that information before we go on with the supplementary estimates.
That was the kind of information we got at that time. With regard to the particular line under discussion at the moment, I remember that the -Canadian Pacific asked for running rights or for co-operation in the construction of the line that the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) was speaking about. The Canadian Pacific to this day have not asked that their plans be approved. They have not spent a dollar on the line. The people in that country are looking for the construction now just as they were five years ago, and unless the Canadian National build it they will still be in the hopeless position of being unable to get the railway facilities that they need. The provision is there in the Statutes of 1919 for cooperation or running rights, and that applies as well to-day as it did then. But are these people to be asked to wait forever for the Canadian Pacific to build, or are they to get the accommodation which will justify their deciding to remain in the country? That is the question that is before this committee. When my hon. friend says he is not speaking for or against the Canadian Pacific Railway I want to say I do not believe there is a member in this House who does not fully realize that the success of the Canadian Pacific is just as essential for the welfare of Canada as the success of the Canadian National. The failure of the Canadian Pacific would mean more to us than the failure of the

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
Canadian National. We have already grappled with that question, and we know that the failure of the Canadian Pacific would be a calamity to this country. There is no hon. member who wants that to happen. There is no hon. member who wants to stand in the way of the Canadian Pacific Railway getting every branch line which it is able to build within what might reasonably be called its own territory, any more than there are hon. members who do not want to see the Canadian National build branch' lines in what is regarded as Canadian National territory. My hon. friend talks about keeping the Canadian Pacific out. Before he opposes this branch line he should go to the people in that district who have been labouring under the hardship of hauling their grain long distances during the years that they have been waiting for railway accommodation.

I am very glad to know
that the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) realizes the necessity of railway transportation in this part of the country. He is anxious that we shall have no duplication; I am just as anxious. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as the last speaker mentioned, have not built any of the railway through country covered by this resolution. The line does not touch Lloydminster but is twenty miles south of that town. I mentioned a few moments ago that there is a large country that needs these facilities, not only north of the present Canadian N'aJ-tional line, running northwest from Lloydminster, but also a large territory to the south of that line. I understand it is the present intention of the Canadian Pacifiic Railway Company to go north to Lloydminster, then in a northwesterly direction to Whitford lake, then south to Vegreville. If we do not want to have any duplication we can easily serve the whole of that country with railway transportation by leaving to the Canadian National the territory from Llodyminster through to Whitford lake and letting the other railway, the Canadian Pacific, go west instead of north from where they are. It would serve a country badly in need of railway facilities, at present not served by the Canadian National, and the Canadian Pacific line would go to its terminus at Vegreville. Both railways would thus have a territory to themselves; there would be no duplication, and the people who are so badly in need of railway facilities would get the necessary service. If these two lines were operated, there is not the slightest doubt in my mind that that country would develop by leaps and bounds and that thousands of people who are 75
at present undecided what to do would make up their minds to stay in that country. There is quite a good country between Vermilion and Wainwright which this southern line would go through, should the Canadian Pacific see fit to go westward instead of northward to Llodyminster.
The hon. member for Centre Vancouver said he did not believe that Sir Henry Thornton himself was in favour of some of the branch lines dealt with in the resolutions which the minister is bringing down. I can only say that the hon. member must have been out of the House the other day when the Minister of Railways read a long letter written by Sir Henry Thornton and addressed to himself, advocating very strongly every railway proposal that was being put forward in these resolutions.

I am somewhat interested in this line, as it goes out of my constituency at Llodyminster. As to the controversy between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I want to say this: The Canadian Pacific are building from the east westward. Up to last year their line stopped at Cut Knife. Two years ago they got an extension of their charter to build from Cut Knife to Lloydminster, and it is suggested that they go on west by a joint arrangement with the national road. They built under that extension forty miles last year from Cut Knife to the Battle river south of Lloydminster, a little more than forty miles, and they advise me that they are now at work extending their line on into Lloydminster, which they expect to reach this summer. Then they propose to go on to the northwest, under the joint arrangement with the national road. An agreement in this connection is incorporated in the statute. It is suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Spencer) that they go south and miss Lloydminster. Now, that would disappoint my people very much. The people at Lloydminster are exceedingly anxious to have these railway facilities,'of which they stand very much in need. I was there last season with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They have five elevators draining a territory thirty miles in diameter and at that time every elevator was full. The men came in there from the northwest country, some from points thirty-five miles distant, and in some cases their wagons were standing along the street-they could not unload. It is a very fertile country, and they are very much in need of this railway.
As to the extension south from the Battle river through to Wainwright or Vermilion, they will not make it, and that is ail there is to it. The Canadian Pacific will not build

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

through that country, because it is not a very good country. The north country is a very good country, and they are ready to go ahead in co-operation with the National line and make an arrangement for running rights over the road. It seems to me under the circumstances that that is the proper thing to do. I am not here as the advocate of the Canadian Pacific interests, but I am here in favour of fair play. This arrangement was made and embodied in a statute, and under that arrangement they have gone on and built their line from Cut Knife to Battle river and they are still building, and they insist that they should have the right to go over the road they originally laid out, and which was sanctioned by parliament. They will not build on the south as suggested by the hon. member for Battle River. They are ready to build through Lloydminster, and Lloydminster wants the Canadian Pacific very badly.

I have been listening to this discussion for some time, though I was not here during the early part of it. One of the curses in this country, it seems to me, has been the duplication of railways. I was looking at a map of this proposed branch line, and also at a map of the proposed Canadian Pacific line, and if both were built it would be an absolute duplication throughout. I am very much in sympathy with the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. McConica), because the duplication of lines is an economic waste. I believe the principle which should be upheld by the government and by the people of Canada in connection with our National Railway, and by the Canadian Pacific as well, is that where it is possible to give running rights to the other road over a section where duplication could be avoided in that way that should be done. It would result in a large monetary saving to the country. Take, for example, my own section of the country. From the head of the lakes down through that north country, where traffic is light, there are three railways, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Certainly two of these would have been amply sufficient, and possibly only one, if it was double-tracked, could handle all the traffic if running rights had been given to the other road. I believe such a policy should be upheld by this government, by the Canadian National and by the Canadian Pacific. In fact, I think it should! be forced on the two railways so far as possible where there is a thinly populated section; one should be permitted to build, or even be forced to build, and the other should be given running rights 
over that piece of road. I think fhat would result in a great economic saving to the country.
With regard to these railways being before the committee, I was on the Railway committee when the two railways were before us and arguments were made for the building of this very line, and as read by the -hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and as I rememberr myself, the Canadian Pacific was compelled when being given the right to build to give running rights to the Canadian National. If that was a compulsory rule put upon them it seems to me that if now the Canadian National is being given the right to build here, the same rule should be reversed and the Canadian Pacific be given running rights over the Canadian National line if built.
Is it not reciprocal?
I do not understand that it is. I understood from the remarks of some hon. members that it was not. I would ask the minister if it is reciprocal.

I think the question which my hon. friend is discussing is set out in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's bill. I pointed out before my hon. friend came in that the Canadian Pacific was now asking that a similar clause be inserted in the bill being granted to the Canadian National, and I further pointed out that it would be perfectly in order to have full consideration of that proposition when we get into committee on the bill, but that it could not very well- be done on the resolution.

I am not attempting to delay the minister in getting into the bill stage, but these thoughts have come to my mind and I thought I would present them now because I might not be here when we are in committee on the bill. I think it is exactly as the hon. minister has explained it, and as was read by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and confirmed by the remarks of other speakers, that a clause was put into the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's bill compelling them to give running rights to the Canadian National. I think the arrangement should be reciprocal. Now that the Canadian National are being given rights, and if, as the hon. member for Battleford says, the Canadian Pacific have built in the past year some forty miles of this line, I think there is justice coming to the Canadian Pacific and that they should be given the same privilege.

The Canadian Pacific have not built forty miles from Lloydminster west, but are now twenty miles south of that town.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

But the hon. member for Battleford said that the intention was to build to Lloydminster and that the people of Lloydminster wanted the Canadian Pacific very badly. Under these circumstances I think it should be the policy of this government and of parliament to make running rights reciprocal wherever possible, in order to save the economic waste which is so rampant in this country through the duplication of lines all over Canada. We have running from here to Montreal three different lines; from Montreal to Toronto three different lines; through my section of the country three different lines. You can look out of the car window and see another line of railway only about a hundred yards away almost wherever you go. We have this unnecessary duplication all over the country, and I just wish to put myself on record as saying that if the Canadian Pacific are being forced in their bill to give running rights, the Canadian National should also be forced to give reciprocal rights to the Canadian Pacific.

I feel that I am well
acquainted with that part of the country. I know it better than I do the city of Ottawa. I have been all through it from Bruederheim to Lloydminster. There are some features of this case that have not been pointed out to the committee properly; perhaps they have been overlooked. That district is as good as any that can be found in Alberta, and that means as good as any in Canada in my opinion. It looks perhaps as if it was not too far between the Canadian National and the St. Paul branch, but the country is a little different from the ordinary. These people who are most anxious to get this road are living south of the Saskatchewan river, which is in a deep valley and it is very hard to cross the river with a heavy load. They could not cross that river economically and get to the railroad on the north, so consequently they have to go south to the Canadian National, which is from thirty to forty miles, and, I think in some cases, more. It is an easy place to build a railway. I have been out over the grade and I know that forty-five miles of the road have been graded. There is, as I say, no better country in Canada, but we want these people to be prosperous. It is not a question of a seven or eight mile haul; it is a question of whether we are going to do what is necessary to allow these people to make a living and make their own homes in that part of the country and become prosperous, and that is what we want to do. On account of the river being on the north, and there being such a deep canyon, they have to go south, and that 75i
makes it farther for them to reach the railroad than it would ordinarily be if the country was level all the way between the two railways. I do not care to take up the time of the House in discussing this, but I wanted to point this out because I know this country well.
There are no branch lines of railways being built in my constituency, and I am sorry because of that fact. There are districts where they are needed but perhaps branch lines will be built later. However, I wanted to give my evidence as to the need of this particular railway, and to express my belief that its construction will be amply justified. I know that the settlers throughout the district are a good class of people, and if you are going to build branch railways you could not put one in a better place. As conditions now are the people there cannot go to the north to get to the other line. Consequently they have to go much farther than they would if the contour of the country were of a different character. For the reasons stated I wished to advocate the construction of this line.
Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil)^:	I simply
want to say that very frequently when a member of the government addresses the committee and gives his viewpoint on a particular subject it is looked upon as imparting to the question a political aspect. We have had a lecture addressed to us to-night on the political aspect of the make up of the Canadian National Railway Board.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am glad that my hon. friend has awakened to a realization of the situation.
I think everybody knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not intend to defend the board, but I think in fairness to hon. members who represent various constituencies their statements should have some value when they are given in all honour and all candour to this House. Personally, I have always been prepared to accept such statements at their proper value, and I think most hon. members have the same idea. There can be no political aspect to a question such as this. We want'to make the Canadian National Railways a success. It is regrettable in the extreme that the question of politics has been introduced at all. The question involved here is whether or not the particular lines under discussion are required, and many hon. gentlemen have declared that they know these lines are necessary. So far as this particular line is concerned, it has been under
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

consideration for years. Part of the line was built from the village of Bruederheim many years ago. It circles to the north following the contour of the Saskatchewan river. The intention at first was to build the road to join the parent line at Vermilion. Since that time it has been extended to Lloydminster. Let me say that I agree heartily with what my hon. friends have said about the desirability of preventing duplication, of which we have had entirely too much in the past. I think in fairness to the National line, and that has been stated on many occasions, it would be well if an arrangement could be made between the two companies,-that is to say between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific,- by which each should confine its activities to its own territory. We all know that the Canadian Pacific are desirous of reaching the city of Edmonton, and that is a laudable desire on their part. But the territory over which, my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) points out, they secured a charter to build, is Canadian National territory, there can be no denying that fact, and if running rights are to be given the logical thing to do would be to give the preference in construction to the Canadian National line and grant the running rights to the Canadian Pacific. I think that would be a thoroughly sensible solution of the matter. My hon. friend will realize at once that the Canadian National then would have a priority right in the picking up of local freight. Let me say too that from my knowledge of the locality and of the line it is not for the branch line they require running rights but for the existing line. There would be a greater mileage by diverting the contour of this line than is the case under the line proposed to be built. I most heartily support the idea of preventing duplication and, where necessary, running rights should be had over either one of these systems by any company desirous of reaching the city of Edmonton, and that city is the objective of the Canadian Pacific. I merely rose to make this statement. I would most heartily support the Canadian Pacific in getting running rights to Edmonton which, I think, is their objective.

Suppose we pass this
legislation without any great objection or scrutiny. The Canadian National Railway then go ahead with this line, but the Canadian Pacific are already constructing in that district.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, not in
that district.

Their line through Cut
Knife and Lloydminster to Edmonton is contained in their charter.
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.J

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They have
not built one foot of line in the province of Alberta up to date as far as my knowledge goes.

What I am pointing out
is this: The Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National fought this out before the Railway committee in 1919. At that time the Canadian Pacific secured the right to construct north-westward from Cut Knife, through Lloydminster, north of the existing Canadian National line, between that and the Saskatchewan river to Edmonton. I remember very well that contour maps and other data were brought before the committee and it was demonstrated, just as was said a while ago, that the canyon of the Saskatchewan river made traffic northward and southward impossible, so the settlers along the south bank of that river had to drive farther to the south and could not get directly across to the railway which was on the north side, or some distance away to the north. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have that charter, and they are now constructing that road northward from where the river has to be crossed. Suppose we go ahead and calmly grant this right to the Canadian National Railway. Then there is nothing to prevent the two of them from constructing other roads through that territory.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it
should be prevented.

Certainly it should.
Furthermore, in 1919 the decision reached by the committee was that the company to go into that country first and construct should be the one that should go through, and running rights should be given to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will recollect that 45 miles of Canadian National line have been constructed from Bruederheim.

The minister refers to
that short distance from Edmonton northeastward?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
From
Bruederheim on the Canadian National railway running in a north easterly direction, taking in a loop of the river, the idea at first being to join the main line again at Vermilion. But since that time the line has been extended in order to reach Lloydminster and give the settlers who are thirty miles from the main line a service.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
That is at the Edmonton end?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

But we are speaking of
the construction northwestward from Lloyd-minster.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I doubt if
the line spoken of by my hon. friend is within thirty miles of Lloydminster at the moment. It will have to be built to Lloydminster and then construction must be commenced in Alberta where this line we are now considering is to commence and of which 45 miles have been built.

What we are asked to do is to authorize the construction of this line.
I am looking at the resolution before the committee. It does not refer to the south end of it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It refers to
45 miles.

It refers to a "Canadian
National Railway line from Lloydminster to the province of Saskatchewan in a generally northwesterly direction to a point in or near Torwship 53 or 54, Range 6, west of 4th, Meridian, in the province of Alberta." Now that is simply a short distance from Lloydminster, northwest of it, and has nothing to do with the other end of the line at all. What I am getting at is this: We ought to be mighty sure that the Canadian Pacific Railway are not actually going in there this year before we recklessly grant what is proposed here. Suppose the Oanadian Pacific Railway are actually constructing from where they left off on the Battle river crossing, what they call the Cut Knife to Melfort branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would
be westward from Cut Knife.
If they are actually constructing and intending to continue this year-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are.

- then there is no need for the National Railways to step into the same territory and start construction. Let me again point out that in 1919, when we discussed this question for several days before the committee, the general decision of the committee was that we would safeguard in the Canadian Pacific Railway bill the rights of the Canadian National Railways which we did, and it is in the statute which I read this evening, but that the railway that would get in and
construct a line first and give the service to the settlers, should have the right to construct. That is the decision we arrived at. I remember the discussion quite distinctly. I say if the Canadian Pacific Railway are actually going to do it-and we ought to know that for a certainty-they should be permitted to go ahead and construct this line, and this resolution should not be passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend, I say that in 1919 this forty-five miles of railway was completed up to-Bruederheim. I have lived in that country for the last fifteen years, and I never heard, of any other location for that line than from. Bruederheim around, taking the circle, and coming back to the main line at Vermilion. Afterwards that was changed, as I pointed out, and it was arranged to run further east and join the main line at Lloydminster. I desire to repeat now that I think it would be well to confine these roads to their own territory. At the moment the1 National Railway is pulling every pound of freight out of that territory, because the National Railway is north of the Saskatchewan river. Every pound of freight that originates in that territory is freight belonging to the National Railways, and I cannot very well understand why a committee of parliament as late as 1919 should have been willing to hand over that territory to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Frankly,
I do not understand it. I would be glad to support a proposition to give running rights to the Canadian Pacific Railway into the city of Edmonton, either over the main line track, or if preferable over the branch line; but I think that the Canadian National line is entitled to that freight, and to the ownership of that line; and, by the ownership of it, entitled to the freight that is gathered from station to station along the line. I would not in the slighest degree put anything in the way of the Canadian Pacific Railway getting into Edmonton, which is the objective point, and would be quite willing to insist on the National Railways giving them running rights, in order to carry on their business. They are entitled to that; and in that case there would be no duplication. I know the country very well and I say I am more than friendly to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think they are a great institution, and I think they are entitled to get a fair show in every territory in which it is logical and right for them to be operating, and which is contiguous to their main line; but I do think that, in all fairness, this territory rightfully belongs to the National Railways. I hope I have made myself clear.	.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

The . minister is giving
utterance to some positive statements. If the government will say, "No, so far as our control is concerned, the Canadian Pacific Railway shall not go into that territory," then the Canadian Pacific will understand what they mean. But, in spite of the fact that the minister does not understand why it was done I tell him that in 1919 it was done by an act of this parliament, after mature consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The committee must have known that there was an agreement in existence.

Certainly, they had all
the information before the committee. The matter was thereshed out in detail after hearing both sides. But the point was-and I remember distinctly-that the Canadian National Railways were not in a position to declare that they would construct that line, and that was the difficulty. I remember very clearly that we declared that the settlers of that district were entitled to service. It was clearly pointed out to the committee that the peculiar conformation of the country, caused by the Saskatchewan river valley, made it not only desirable but absolutely necessary that the settlers should have service, and that was the reason the committee decided to admit of a competition, if you like, as to who should get in first.
In reply to what the minister has said, let me come back to the point again: If it is shown that the Canadian Pacific are prepared to build in there now, I say they ought to be permitted to build for two reasons, first, in order that we may keep faith with the Canadian Pacific Railway in relation to the arrangement discussed in 1919; and, secondly that this government and country do not require to look for places to spend money. If we can possibly avoid expenditures we ought to do so. As to the ownership of territory, I do not think it is applicable to this case, because it was threshed out and decided five years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
feel like giving way to my hon. friend's argument, except in so far as it is applicable. If the Canadian National Railways as he stated-and I want to quote him correctly-[DOT] were not prepared to build, then I can understand why the committee were induced to grant that charter but my hon. friend said on one or two occasions that there was a dispute about it and that the first man on the ground was going to get the right to build. If that is the case, I can hardly understand the attitude of the Canadian National Railways 
with respect to that matter, and I hardly understand why on the other end of the loop, the forty-five miles upon which money has been spent, should be abandoned.

Pardon me, they are not
abandoning it. They switch off there at

I cannot see the name on the map.
Bruederheim.

Yes, that is the point
my hon. friend refers to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That was
the starting point.

It runs from Edmonton
to Bruederheim, and swings down to Lloyd-minster. There is no loose end there. It does not matter one iota what they started out to do; they may have started out to make a larger map; I have no doubt they did, but there is no loose end there, or turning southward to Lloydminster. So that there is no need for the Canadian National, so far as that is concerned.

I might say that the
Canadian Pacific railway is not built from Edmonton to Bruederheim, nor does this old Canadian Northern grade start from Edmonton. It begins at Bruederheim running east from there towards Lloydminster. The Canadian Pacific proposed road is coming in from the east by Whitford lake, then, I presume, crosses the Canadian Nation'al line near Bruederheim running into Edmonton on the south side of the river where the Canadian National main line crosses the Saskatchewan river at Eork Saskatchewan.

The Minister of the
Interior made a remark which might be misinterpreted. I was on the committee he refers to. He said he did not understand why the committee should have given the rights to the Canadian Pacific Railway at that time, because it was really Canadian National Railway territory. I remember some of the discussion before the committee, and my recollection of it is that the Canadian Pacific came forward and asked for rights to build into that territory. They were opposed by the Canadian Northern Railway. For some reason we had all these questions before the committee. Mr. Hanna was here on behalf of the Canadian Northern and Mr. Coleman appeared for the Canadian Pacific Railway. Mr. Ruel the counsel was here; the Canadian Pacific solicitors were also present and they fought it out. If I recollect correctly, it was stated that the Canadian Northern Railway

was not ready financially to go ahead, with the proposition, and the Canadian Pacific was. I do not know whether the Canadian Northern had their charter then or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That was
the time they got it.

However that was the
ground that was taken. It was a very hard fight because the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway fought the matter very hard. It was the opinion of the committee and of parliament that the Canadian Pacific Railway had the right to build. Parliament gave the Canadian Pacific Railway a charter to build. They have not done so except in the southern part. But in the charter we inserted a clause compelling the Canadian Pacific Railway to give running rights to the Canadian Northern, which at that time, I think, was a perfectly fair and legitimate proposition to both railways. I do not remember, but I doubt very much if the Canadian Pacific was agreeable to the insertion of this clause. To-day, if we are going to take away from the Canadian Pacific the right of building in that country,-certainly one railway is quite sufficient there-and permit the Canadian National to build, it is only right that a reciprocal arrangement should be provided for and the Canadian Pacific treated in the same way as the old Canadian Northern was formerly treated. The minister nods his head, and I assume he agrees with me. I think a whole lot of time might be saved if he would accept the suggestion which has come from practically all over the House, that before this bill comes down he will ascertain the attitude of the two railways and see if running rights cannot be arranged which will be satisfactory for this particular line and will also probably be satisfactory throughout the whole district. Lloydminster would be satisfied according to what my hon. friend from Battleford (Mr. McConica) says. It seems to me that would be a fair proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have only this to say. It would be absolutely useless to give running rights over this line to the Canadian National railways. Why should they have to make a detour for all their through business and haul it over a greater mileage than on their main line? The case is absolutely the reverse with the Canadian Pacific. If the latter go in there they take territory which is now all Canadian National and they would control that territory and gather the freight. Running rights would merely be for through traffic from one end of the line to
the other which would be of no value to the Canadian National whatever because they would not be permitted to do logical business if the Canadian Pacific built the line. I am not arguing against the Canadian Pacific for a moment I am simply pointing out what is obvious to anyone who is familiar with the territory.

Does the minister say it
would be no use to give running rights to the Canadian Pacific.?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; it would be no use to give running rights to the Canadian National.
I am saying the proposition is to give the Canadian National the right to build the road and to give the Canadian Pacific running rights over it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
different.
I have already asked the heads of the two railways to get together on this matter. The time for consideration of this will be when the legislation is in bill form.

You should have told us
that an hour ago.

Yes an hour and a half
ago.

Mr. Chairman, I
am somewhat surprised at the lack of information supplied regarding many of these lines. It is a slow process to obtain information. I could not help admiring the earnestness with which the Minister of the Interior tried to impress upon the committee the fact that when a member declared that a road in his constituency was desirable, the declaration in itself should be pretty hear sufficient to justify construction. I am confident that every member could find strong arguments to justify railway construction in his constituency. The Canadian National system is owned by the people and any expenditure must be met by them. The great difficulty seems to be to arrive at a clear understanding as to whether a line is justifiable or not. In the old days there was keen competition between the railways for traffic, although there was no competition as to rates. To-day it is very important that we safeguard ourselves against undue railway duplication. I think there are many lines in operation to-day that might be properly closed and the traffic carried over one road. It does not matter whether it is a privately-owned or a government-owned railway, we must have lower railway rates or we cannot prosper. But we cannot have lower
C.NH.-Branch Lines

rates if we build unnecessary railway mileage. This country is not in a position to build roads that are not absolutely essential. When I hear hon. members from the West arguing that because they are eight or ten miles from a railway it is desirable that there should be a further construction undertaken, I can assure the committee that there are many sections in the old provinces where the people have not as good railway facilities as those enjoyed in the West.
I protest against this lack of information. It is evident that if we are to make a success of the Canadian National Railways some different method must be adopted in regard to the building of branch lines than that which is now being followed. There is no closing our eyes to the fact that the board of directors have been largely appointed for political reasons rather than for any especial qualifications or railway knowledge. That being the case, there is suspicion among the people that something of a political nature is attached to these proposals. It is well known that there were negotiations between representative men of western Canada and the government before parliament assembled; in fact, it has been said that a bargain was made between them. Well, I think we have good evidence of it in the docile manner in which hon. members to my left stultify themselves and vote contrary to what they openly profess in this House. They have done that repeatedly during this session. Their actions would indicate that they are very anxious to secure more branch lines in western Canada. One hon. member even had the hardihood to compare expenditure in rural mail delivery in some of the old provinces with that in western Canada, but he did not take the precaution, or was not fair enough, to give the revenues in these old provinces compared with similar revenues in western Canada. In some sections of northern Ontario which have been recently opened up, and where rich mineral deposits have been uncovered, there is possibly more need of railway facilities than in those districts to which reference has been made. Yet we are absolutely handicapped and cannot proceed because the province of Ontario has undertaken to build development roads, and therefore is not in a position to give the railway facilities which the people there are entitled to. This simply means that the province will have to dispose of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to the federal government in order to have feeders built, because that great section tributary to the railway must have railway facilities if it is to go ahead.

speechtext: Is it not a fact that through lines have been built right across Ontario, both by the Canadian Pacific and by the government of Canada? The Canadian National, the old Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific were built directly across northern Ontario.

speechtext: Have branch lines ever been asked for?

Is that all you have to do?
Some hon. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

speechtext:

If there is a political representative on the board that may account for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
(Argenteuil):	I do not
know that any member of the board particularly asked for any of these lines. But let me ask my hon. friend:	What is the
political affiliation of Mr. James Stewart of Winnipeg? I have never heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:

He is a gentleman who
unfortunately seldom attends the board. If these men were more regular in their attendance we should be able to get the advantage of their knowledge and skill; but the trouble is that the board is in the hands of half a dozen pseudo politicians.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend has answered his own question, I think. ~ He has practically said that the members do not attend the board and he is content with Sir Henry Thornton.
The minister admits that there are no branch lines in northern Ontario and from his remarks I would infer that there is no necessity for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not
say so, sir. I do not know the situation.

I have been endeavouring to emphasize the fact that there

C.N.It.-Branch Lines
are points in (that mineral belt that are very much in need of railway accommodation which they are not receiving. There is not one mile of railway to be built in Ontario so far as can be seen at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have
simply been asking for information. My hon. friend remarked that nothing had been done for Ontario and I pointed out that certain lines crossed northern Ontario. Although there may be no branch lines, surely my hon. friend will admit that a line circling the Lake of the Woods to the south is serving a large area of country. And that line belongs to the Canadian National Railways. Surely he will agree that the Grand Trunk Pacific, crossing right through the heart of the north country, is of some value to the people up there.

The territory to
which I am referring is the mineral belt between Cochrane and Englehart to which the Canadian National is not tributary, and that is the section of the country that is now so much in need of railway facilities. It is true that a branch line of the Canadian National Railways could be built down into that locality, but a better service would be rendered if a line were built from the road that is now owned and which was built by the province of Ontario. For that reason I state that if this policy is to continue there is nothing to be done but for the government to assume that road that has been constructed by the province. The Canadian National Railways have running rights over that road and the interests of that country demand that something be done to enable development to proceed. The wealth of the country there would indicate that such development is possible if railway facilities are provided.

The hon. member for
Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is not here, but the Minister of Railways will no doubt be able to answer the question which I am about to ask and which I intended to direct to the hon. member. What year was it that the bill was introduced to provide for branch lines construction which the hon. member for Pontiac stated that the government then in power refused to refer to the Railway committee?

I suggest that my hon.
friend wait until the hon. member for Pontiac returns. I did not refer to any bill that was introduced for the construction of branch lines. Certain branch lines were to be taken over under the Appropriation Act
of 1920 for which 848,000,000 was appropriated, and my contention was that no information was given to the House, as far as I could recollect, concerning these branch lines as to cost and territory, to the extent that I am affording the committee now.

Did the minister say,
in 1920?

I think it was in 1920; I had Hansard a moment ago. But my argument was not directed to anything that had happened in the committee, nor did it refer to the question whether any bill should be sent to the committee or not. I was simply contending that we were giving loads of information now that had not been given heretofore.

I see the hon. member
for Pontiac is back now, and perhaps he will answer the question I asked a moment ago. What year was it that the bill was introduced by the late government to provide for the construction of branch lines, which bill was refused to be submitted to the Railway committee?
I think it was in 1919, in either the first or the second session.
There was no such bill introduced at all; the hon. member was talking without the book.
In the Grand Trunk bill there was a section providing for the construction of 44 branch lines.
What Grand Trunk bill?

The Grand Trunk bill;
there was provision for the purchase of 44 branch lines in the West. We asked that these 44 lines be considered in detail, and that request was not only refused but the section was passed under closure.
That is my recollection.

My hon. friend says that his recollection is that in the Grand Trunk bill there was power to acquire 44 branch lines in western Canada. The suggestion is so absurd that I would insult the House if I denied it. In 1920 there was provision in the estimates for branch lines, and we plead with this government to do what we did then. All that the government need do is follow our example and we shall be satisfied.
Will you take the information that you then gave?

Yes, I shall be content with such information.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines
Which was nothing.

The hon. member must have had a bad dream. I do not know what hon. gentlemen behind the minister have in their heads at all, but there was no such clause in the Grand Trunk acquisition legislation. That legislation was merely to provide for the acquirement of the Grand Trunk Railway. There was a previous bill for the acquirement of branch lines, but that was long before 1920, and 'it was for the acquirement of certain lines, that were constructed, which of course is a different thing. Now, as respects the minister's allegation that no information was given, and the specific allegation just now that no information was given as to estimated cost and as to territory, I will undertake to provide the minister with that information and to show that it was given. I know that no such information was refused; I know that it was given at some stage of the bill, although I cannot say at what precise juncture. I stand here to say that hon. members will have difficulty-indeed I do not think they will find it possible -to produce an instance in which specific information asked for was not given in respect of the legislation referred to by the minister. I can well recall these
11	p.m occasions, because I know how active the member for Pontiac was; and I have read some of his speeches. I would ask the House to go back over these days and read the debates; do not let hon. gentlemen refer to one little stage of the bill.
This is the bill.
That is the wrong bill.
The hon. member has got wrong information this time.
I get wrong information from hon. gentlemen opposite.
No, from gentlemen behind you.

Not at all; I get right information there, but this is not the bill mentioned by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). The Canadian National Railways Act of 1919 is not the act for the acquirement of the Grand Trunk. There is a schedule the purport of which I do not know at the moment, but it may be that to which the hon. gentleman refers. There could be no such legislation in the Grand Trunk Acquisition Act. I will look over the schedule to the Canadian National Railway Act and speak to it a minute later; of course I cannot do it while I am on my feet.

I understand that a good
deal of the opposition to this branch line is due to the fact that the Canadian Pacific has a charter in this connection, secured in 1919. The member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) suggested that the charter was granted to the Canadian Pacific at that time on account of the Canadian National being unprepared to proceed with the construction. The fact that the Canadian Pacific have not done anything with that road shows that they were not any more prepared to start with the construction than were the Canadian National. I think the time has come when any railway company applying for a charter should be prepared to put up a guarantee or bond that they are going to start construction, and that should be done before any charter is granted by this House. I would like to confirm what the Minister of the Interior said in regard to this territory belonging to the Canadian National. The present Canadian National line parallels the Saskatchewan river and all the territory north of that line runs to the river, which has very deep banks. All the business coming from that- territory comes now to the Canadian National, and if the Canadian Pacific secured a charter through there it would simply spoil the whole business for the Canadian National. The Canadian Pacific built last year from Cut Knife, I believe, a distance of about thirty miles, and they are still a considerable distance from Lloyd-minster. I presume this year's construction will take them into Lloydminster and then they will be able to secure running rights over the Canadian National from there to Edmonton, so they will not be inconvenienced, I am glad the construction of this branch line is proposed this year, because the settlers of that district have been looking for it since 1909. Farmers there have told me that they were prepared to go out and give their labour free if they could only get this road started. I am glad, I say, that the board have seen fit to recommend the starting of construction on this line during the present season, and I hope it will be pushed to an early completion.

Referring to the statutes
of Canada, 1919, Chapter 13, the clause I was alluding to is clause 20, which reads as follows:
The times for the commencement and completion of the construction of the lines of railway specified in the second schedule to this act, which certain of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern system were authorized to construct, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this act.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
If my right hon. friend will read the second schedule he will see that a full list of the railways is there given. When we asked for information, and asked an opportunity to study each or any special branch line in particular, by a committee or otherwise, we were refused, and the clause was passed under closure.

Well, I am delighted
that the hon. member has found the clause. This Canadian National Railway Act was not the act, first of all, by which the Grand Trunk was acquired; that was done under the Grand Trunk Acquisition Act. However, that is merely a matter of name. The Canadian National Railway Act was the act by which we consolidated all the roads at that time owned by the state-that is, roads that were acquired by stock interest. They were all made into one system, and provision was made for the appointment of a directorate and their operation as one. Consequently such roads as the various constituent companies had, already the property of the state, became consolidated in the possession of one company of which the state held the ownership. Then the clause to which my hon. friend refers provided that the times for the commencement and completion of lines already authorized and specified in the second schedule-
-which certain of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern system were authorized to construct, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this act.
The various companies, when private companies, had the right to construct those roads mentioned in the schedule. The private companies are now owned by the state, and the state when consolidating these companies, extends the time within which that construction may go on. The state does not come to parliament and ask for a dollar to go on, or bind itself to go on, or express any intention of going on.

I never contended that
either.

It merely extends for its own benefit the right to construct which the original companies obtained. What in the world would be the sense in such a case of going to a committee? Now the hon. member has revealed just about the character of the obstruction we were subjected to. The House was kept day and night over a clause that merely reserved to the state the right to go on if parliament authorized it to do so and voted the money to do so later on. This was merely a keeping alive of charter rights that had already been accorded to a private
company. That is what they forced closure on in this House. Could anything better illustrate the character of the opposition we had? We would have had to come back to parliament to get the money before we could build a line, and in every case we came in the constitutional way and had the money voted in estimates. Now, I wonder what is to be thought of an opposition that held parliament by the throat, talked against time all day and all night, forcing closure in order that a clause of that sort might be got through?

If these had remained
private companies, had they not been taken over by the government and had they wished to have their time extended as was done under this act, would they not have been compelled to come before the Railway committee?

Very good. But we
would have had to come to parliament later for the money anyway, but a private company would not have had to come to parliament for the money. The private company would vote the money itself and go on; that is exactly the point. What on earth was the common sense of sending that clause to a committee, a clause that merely reserved the right to go on, merely kept the charters alive for the benefit of the state, when as a matter of fact, if we should decide later to go on with even a single branch we would have had to come back to parliament for every cent of the money?
Mr, CANNON: J am not discussing the question whether it should have been referred to a committee. But the right hon. gentleman asked that one instance be pointed out where his government refused information,, and I have quoted one. We asked for information and we were refused it; that is the point.
What was the information asked for there?
As to the revival of forty charters. I think parliament was entitled to some information as to where the railways were to be built, and so on.
What was the information asked for?

The information asked
was as to where the railways were to be built, the merits of each of the charters, the expenditures that we might be called upon to make in the future, and so on. With respect to every one of the questions put by the opposition at that time the government refused to give any enlightenment. That is the point before the committee.
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

This is getting better all the time. I rose first to answer the statement that we had refused to allow bills similar to these, providing for new construction, to go to a committee. This was given as the instance. I do not need now to review the argument; hon. gentlemen opposite are simply exposed. Now the hon. member says, " Oh, you refused to give information then, refused to tell us where the lines were going, what was to be the cost, and so on." Well, I have no recollection of the refusal, but we will assume it was done, if that will help the argument any. What on earth would that information have to do with the wisdom of maintaining the charters alive, when we owned the charters? That is the character of information that was asked. That was the character of information in respect of which parliament was held up, the time of the people wasted, the time of members wasted, whole nights consumed-just in order to make a demonstration, to try to create the impression that information was not given. That character of information had not the slightest thing on earth to do with the wisdom of passing the clause. The clause was manifestly wise in the first place. Nobody could get any benefit from it except the state. If it was providing money with which to go ahead as this bill is, certainly we should have given that information. When we asked for money and expressed any intention of going on at all we came on later and gave the information.

It is only fair that before buying charters we should know what we are taking over. When my right hon. friend was Prime Minister he was buying all kinds of things without knowing what he was purchasing, but we want to know what we ire buying when we are paying out public noney.

We were not giving anything for the charters. We already owned them, and were merely by legislation keeping them alive. They are all set out here and everything about them is given. I am prepared to leave the matter with the committee.
